Composed by State Preceptor Bojo Jinul of Goryeo.
Annotated by Zhanran.
This very mind of empty stillness and spiritual knowing is your original face.
The Buddha dwells on Vulture Peak — seek him not afar;
the Vulture Peak stands within your mind. Within each person is a tower of the spirit; before that tower, revere and serve.
Take the dharma-body as your own, not the physical body;
take spiritual knowing as your own, not the deluded mind.
One who awakens to this and guards it sits in the one suchness, unmoving and liberated;
one who is deluded about this and turns away from it fares through the six destinies in kalpa-long rebirth.
Effortless stillness and knowing.
The Avatamsaka Sutra,
in its chapter “The Arising of the Tathagata,” says:
“There is not one sentient being who does not possess the Tathagata’s wisdom, but because of deluded thought, inverted and clinging, they do not realize it;
if they were free of deluded thought
, the wisdom of all things, the wisdom that is natural, and the unobstructed wisdom would at once appear.”
if they were free of deluded thought

There are three levels here: the cessation of coarse thoughts, the cessation of subtle thoughts, and even the cessation of exceedingly subtle thoughts. For a person who recites the Buddha’s name, for instance, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts, while the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is a subtle thought. Ordinarily, when both coarse and subtle thoughts have ceased, this is called no-thought, the no-thought of common parlance. Further, if the exceedingly subtle thoughts also come to rest, this is ultimate no-thought. Hence the meaning of the term “no-thought” must be determined from its context. [Exceedingly subtle thoughts] The exceedingly subtle arising and perishing, the flowing and shifting, of the consciousness-mind — this is the mark of the alaya-consciousness. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
“When the bodhisattva’s ground is exhausted
(the ten grounds fully cultivated)
, and the aids to practice are perfected, with a single thought they accord, awaken to the first arising of mind, and the mind has no initial mark;
because they are far removed from exceedingly subtle thoughts,
they perceive the nature of mind
, the mind at once abides forever,
and this is named ultimate enlightenment
Master Guifeng said:
If the exceedingly subtle flow
(exceedingly subtle thoughts)
is utterly stilled

, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment stands alone in clear radiance, then it responds to capacities and manifests a thousand billion bodies to deliver sentient beings who have the conditions,
and this is named Buddha
(See the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp.)

[The wisdom of all things] The wisdom that can know and understand all inner dharmas and inner names, and can likewise know and understand all outer dharmas and outer names. [The wisdom that is natural] The wisdom that arises naturally, without borrowed effort. [The unobstructed wisdom] The wisdom that is free and unobstructed — that is, the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Surangama Sutra says:
“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, continue through birth and death, all because they do not know the permanent true mind, the pure and luminous essence of the nature
(that is, all because they do not know this pure and luminous essence that is the permanent true mind)
, and so employ all manner of deluded thought
(that is, they go and employ deluded thought)
; these thoughts are not true, and so there is the wheel of rebirth.”

[The true mind, the pure and luminous essence of the nature] The pure and luminous essence of the nature is the wondrously luminous essence whose nature is fundamentally pure. Grammatically, “the pure and luminous essence of the nature” is in apposition, qualifying the noun “true mind.” [The wheel of rebirth] Fragmented birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death. [Fragmented birth-and-death] For sentient beings within the three realms and six destinies, because their good and evil karma brings its retribution, their lifespans each have a limit and their bodily forms each have their divisions; hence their birth and death are called “fragmented birth-and-death.” One who ends fragmented birth-and-death escapes the wheel of rebirth. [Transformational birth-and-death] The sages of the three vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended fragmented birth-and-death, in the course of cultivating the Way see deluded thoughts gradually extinguished and realization gradually increase. This passage from delusion to awakening differs in every period, and the shift from an earlier period into a later one is exactly like passing through one birth and death; its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable, and therefore it is named “transformational birth-and-death.” One who ends transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Master Guifeng said:

“All dharmas are like a dream — all the sages say the same. Therefore deluded thoughts are fundamentally still, and the objects of dust are fundamentally empty. The mind of empty stillness is not obscured in its spiritual knowing.
This very knowing of empty stillness is your true nature

. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not borrow from conditions to arise, nor does it arise because of objects. The single word “knowing” is the gate of all wonders. Because from beginningless time they have been deluded about it, beings falsely cling to body and mind as self and give rise to thoughts of greed, anger, and the rest. If one meets a good friend who shows and teaches one, one suddenly awakens to the knowing of empty stillness. Knowing itself is without thought and without form — who then is the mark of self, the mark of person? Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, at once awaken; once awakened, it is at once gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here. Therefore though one cultivates all ten thousand practices in full, one takes no-thought alone as the root. Once one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought, then love and aversion naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses naturally are cut off and removed, and merit and practice naturally advance. Having understood that all marks are no-marks, one is naturally practicing the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death at once come to an end. When arising and perishing have ceased, stillness and illumination appear before one, functioning without limit, and this is named Buddha.”
(The Collected Preface to the Various Explanations of the Source of Chan.)
the knowing of empty stillness

It is also called spiritual knowing. [Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, at once awaken; once awakened, it is at once gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only here] Awakening to the fact that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must at once awaken to the fact that this is taking the illusory as real and being turned about by illusory marks. Once one has awakened to this point, the deluded thought at once disappears. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here!
Jinul (
, corresponding to the Southern Song period in our own country), also written Jinul (
nè

), was the founding patriarch of the Jogye order of Korea. He was a man of Dongju in the western capital region (Seoheung county in Hwanghae province), and his sobriquet was Oxherd. The master’s secular surname was Jeong, and at the age of eight he left home under Chan Master Zonghui of Mount Jogye. After receiving the full precepts, he formed a society with more than ten fellow students to cultivate concentration and wisdom. At twenty-five he passed the monastic examination and resided at Cheongwon Temple in Changpyeong, where he gained an insight through reading the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. At twenty-eight he moved to Bomun Temple on Mount Hagha, where he obtained the Tang-dynasty Li Tongxuan’s Huayan Commentary (that is, the New Huayan Treatise). Combining the essential purport of Chan awakening with the teaching of Huayan, he formed a society at Joju Temple on Mount Palgong, engaged in the actual practice of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure, and composed the Essay Urging the Cultivation of Concentration and Wisdom in Society.

[The full precepts] The precepts that are complete and full, such as the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhiksu and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts of a bhiksuni. [The monastic examination] A system of examinations for monastics implemented from the Goryeo period of Korea to the early Joseon dynasty. It was divided into the order selection and the great selection. The order selection was conducted by the temples, the great selection by the state. Only after passing the order selection could one take part in the great selection. The great selection was divided into the Chan great selection and the doctrinal great selection, the former held at Gwangmyeong Temple, the head temple of the Chan school, and the latter at Wangnyun Temple, the head temple of the doctrinal school. The great selection was held once every three years.

Several years later he withdrew to live in seclusion at the Hermitage of Non-Abiding on Mount Jiri, devoting himself to insight meditation. One day, reading the Recorded Sayings of Dahui, he suddenly had a great awakening. In the third year of King Sinjong (

), he again formed a society at Jixiang Temple on Mount Songgwang, and for eleven years before and after devoted himself to widely proclaiming Jogye Chan, advocating sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation and the equal holding of concentration and wisdom. Thereafter he founded the White Cloud Retreat on Mount Eokbo, the Jicui Hermitage, the Zuyue Hermitage, and others. In the first year of King Huijong (
), he renamed Jeonghye Temple on Mount Songgwang the Seon Cultivation Society on Mount Jogye, and it became the root practice center of Korean Chan.
In the spring of the sixth year of King Huijong (

), the master foreknew the time of his departure. On the night before his parinirvāṇa, while he was bathing, his attendant ceaselessly sought instruction, and the master calmly answered each question in turn. At dawn the next day (the twenty-seventh day of the third month), the assembly came to see him off. The master ordered his attendant to beat the drum and gather the community, then, holding his staff, strode briskly into the dharma hall and ascended the seat to teach. The master said: “The efficacy of Chan is inconceivable. Today I have come here, intending to set before you all this inconceivable mystery, clear and plain. Now ask whatever you wish; this old fellow will surely give each of you an answer.” The assembly asked one after another, and the master responded to each as it came, his eloquence unobstructed. When he had answered the last question, the master tapped his staff on the ground a few times and said: “Say a thousand things, speak ten thousand — it is all right here.” Having spoken, he was calm and unmoved, and passed peacefully into quiescence.

The master’s worldly lifespan was fifty-three years and his dharma-age thirty-six years (that is, thirty-six years from his full ordination); his posthumous title was ‘Buddha-Sun, Universally Illuminating State Preceptor.’ His works include the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, the Essential Selections from the Record of Distinct Practices of the Dharma Collection together with Private Notes, the Treatise on Perfect and Sudden Buddhahood, the Treatise on Resolving Doubts about Watching the Phrase, the Essential Gate of Buddha-Recitation, and the Postscript to the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. His dharma heirs were Huichen, Zhengxuan, Shouyu, and others.
[Li Tongxuan (

)] Known to the world as Elder Li and also as the Date-and-Cypress Great Master, he was a Huayan scholar of the Tang dynasty and a man of Cangzhou (southeast of present-day Cang county in Hebei province). In his youth he delved into the principles of the Yijing; at about forty he devoted himself to Buddhist texts and gave his mind to the Avatamsaka Sutra. It was just then that the “eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka” had been translated. In the spring of the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era (

), carrying the newly translated Avatamsaka Sutra, he went to the home of Gao Shannu in Daxian village, Tongying township, southwest of Meng county in Taiyuan, and composed a treatise to elucidate the sutra’s meaning. For three years he did not leave his door; it is said that each day he ate only ten dates and one cypress-leaf cake in the morning, and from this the world called him the Date-and-Cypress Great Master. He later carried his draft to a cave dwelling at the foot of Mount Shenfu (that is, the cave dwelling on Mount Fang in Shouyang, Taiyuan) and continued writing there, completing the work after five years: this is the forty-fascicle New Huayan Treatise. He then composed the four-fascicle Brief Explanation of the New Huayan Sutra’s Stages of Practice and the Resolution of Doubts. He passed into quiescence on the twenty-eighth day of the third month of the eighteenth year of Kaiyuan (
), or by another account of the twenty-eighth year of Kaiyuan (

); he was ninety-six years old. [The Avatamsaka Sutra] Its full name is the Mahavaipulya Buddhavatamsaka Sutra. It is the cardinal scripture in which the Buddha, after attaining the Way, at the bodhi site and elsewhere, through such great bodhisattvas as Samantabhadra and Manjusri, reveals the causal practices and fruition virtues of the Buddha. There are three Chinese translations of this sutra: First, the translation by Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin, titled the Mahavaipulya Buddhavatamsaka Sutra, in sixty fascicles; to distinguish it from the later Tang translation it is also called the “old translation Avatamsaka,” or the “sixty-fascicle Avatamsaka.” Second, the translation by Siksananda in the Tang dynasty under Empress Wu Zetian, titled the Mahavaipulya Buddhavatamsaka Sutra, in eighty fascicles, also called the “new translation Avatamsaka,” or the “eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka.” Third, the translation by Prajna in the Zhenyuan era of the Tang, also titled the Mahavaipulya Buddhavatamsaka Sutra, in forty fascicles; its full name is the Mahavaipulya Buddhavatamsaka Sutra, Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices Entering the Inconceivable Liberation Realm, abbreviated as the Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices, or called the “forty-fascicle Avatamsaka.”
[The Essentials of Mind Cultivation]

The title of this piece is “The Essentials of Mind Cultivation,” which means: the essential keys of mind cultivation. Its core is to explain why one should cultivate the mind, and how one should go about cultivating the mind. Its guiding purport is:
sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, and the equal holding of concentration and wisdom.
The Essentials of Mind Cultivation is the companion piece to the Direct Explanation of the True Mind. For annotations to the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind

Self-nature is the essence, and mind is the function of self-nature. Mind has two states: the original mind and the consciousness-mind. The original mind is the primordial state of mind: spiritually luminous, penetrating and clear, standing alone in its own right. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“One who does not know the original mind gains no benefit from studying the Dharma. If one knows the original mind and sees one’s own nature, one is named a true person, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”
The consciousness-mind is also called the
clinging-mind

— the mind that arises by clinging to and discriminating the six objects of dust; it is what the Buddha in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment calls the “shadows of the conditions of the six objects of dust.” It is also the mind by which we distinguish and know what is present before us in daily use, that is, the single thought presently before us, whose characteristic is discrimination, calculation, liking and disliking, taking and rejecting. The arising of thoughts and the stirring of mind, and seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing (the “knowing” here is discriminative knowing) — all these are the consciousness-mind at work.
The original mind is undefiled, and so it is also called the intrinsically pure mind. The original mind is without knowing and yet omniscient, and therefore the original mind is also called the
mind of spiritual knowing

. Note carefully: the “knowing” of spiritual knowing is a knowing without grasping at marks; in order to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and perceiving, it is called spiritual knowing. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:
“Prajna is non-knowing — that is, it is without the knowing that grasps at marks.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“To establish knowing upon seeing and hearing is the root of ignorance; when seeing and hearing are without the mark of seeing, this is nirvāṇa, undefiled and truly pure.”
Practice is to settle this scattered consciousness-mind (the clinging-mind) and thereby arrive at the state of the original mind (the mind of spiritual knowing) — as it is said,
“when the mad mind does not rest, its resting is bodhi.”
The Essential Methods of Mind Transmission says:
“When thoughts cease and
(deliberation is)
forgotten, the Buddha appears of himself.”
The Sutra of the Buddha Treasury says:
“The buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is entirely without thought and without conception.”

Practice is to return to the source, to transform the state of the consciousness-mind (the mind that clings to the six objects of dust and discriminates) into the state of the original mind (the mind of empty stillness and spiritual knowing). Awakening is awakening to this mind of empty stillness and spiritual knowing; cultivation is guarding (watching over) this mind of empty stillness and spiritual knowing. First preserve, then let be, until non-doing. Therefore this treatise says:
“Those who awaken to this
(the original mind)
and guard it sit in the one suchness, unmoving and liberated; those who are deluded about this and turn their backs on it fare through the six destinies
(the six paths)
in kalpa-long rebirth.”
It should be noted, however, that in ordinary discussions the essence and the function of the fundamental nature, and delusion and awakening, are each given separate names. For example,
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha

— for convenience of discussion, that article gives separate names to the essence and function of the fundamental nature and to delusion and awakening: self-nature is the essence, and mind is its function. The awakened state of self-nature is named intrinsic nature (tathagatagarbha, buddha-nature); the deluded state of self-nature is named consciousness-nature (the consciousness storehouse). The awakened state of mind is named the original mind (the true mind); the deluded state of mind is named the consciousness-mind (the deluded mind). In the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, however, essence and function are often not distinguished, and delusion and awakening share the same term: all are the one word “true mind,” and self-nature, buddha-nature, mind, true mind, original mind, true suchness, and so on are regarded as different names for one essence. On this point State Preceptor Bojo, in the chapter “Different Names of the True Mind” of his other work, the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, discriminates with great clarity, and says:

“If one penetrates the true mind, all its names are understood; if one is in the dark about this true mind, all its names become hindrances. Therefore with respect to the true mind, one should be most careful and precise.”
(For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind

) Therefore, as for the words “mind,” “true mind,” “buddha-nature,” and so on in the sentences of this text — whether they are essence or function, delusion or awakening — one should identify them clearly according to the context.
The function of mind is incomparably important!
The Verse on the Character for Mind says:
“Three dots appear like stars, one hook like a slanting moon;
(creatures of fur and feather)
issue forth from this — becoming a Buddha too is up to it.”
Master Hanshan said:
“The Buddha said:

’The dharmas above and below the three realms are made by the one mind alone.’ By “above the three realms” are meant the four sage realms beyond the world, namely Buddha, bodhisattva, sravaka, and pratyekabuddha. By “below the three realms” are meant the six-path ordinary beings, namely the three good paths of gods, humans, and asuras, and the three evil paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. Thus within the ten dharma realms, all sages and ordinary beings, all good and evil causes and effects, all dependent and principal adornments, are made by the one mind alone. Yet this one mind is none other than the mind by which we, in our daily use before our eyes, distinguish and know.”
(From the Dream Journey Collection,
Instruction for Xu Qingzhi.)
[Dependent and principal adornments] “Dependent and principal” refers to the

dependent reward and the principal reward. The lands, houses, and implements of the world are what the body depends upon, and are called the “dependent reward”; the body of a sentient being, falsely assembled from the five aggregates, is what past karma has brought forth, and is called the “principal reward.” “Adornment” has two senses: first, the sense of solemn dignity; second, the sense of decoration. To ornament a land with what is good and beautiful, or to ornament the body with merit and virtue, is called adornment — for example, the Buddha Speaks the Amitābha Sutra says: “adorned with merit and virtue.” To heap the body with evil deeds is also called adornment — for example, the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says: “Such a foolish person steals the property of the sangha, steals the property of the sangha of the present, teaches the Dharma impurely, is without shame or remorse, and thus adorns himself with all manner of evil karma.”

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by sentient beings who have the two desires of sex and food; it includes the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below. The realm of form is the world inhabited by sentient beings who are free of the two desires of sex and food but still possess a physical body; it includes the four dhyanas and eighteen heavens. The formless realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who are already without physical body but dwell with mind and consciousness in profound and wondrous meditative concentration; it includes the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of boundless space, the heaven of boundless consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all realms of birth and death, the wheel of rebirth, for ordinary beings; therefore the Buddhist practitioner’s first aim is to transcend the three realms.
The Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karma Paths says:

“Because the mental intentions of sentient beings differ, the karma they create also differs, and thus there is the wheel of rebirth through the various paths. Dragon King! Do you see how in this assembly
(the buddhas, great bodhisattvas, great bhiksus, gods, humans, asuras, and so on in this dharma assembly)
, and in the great ocean, the shapes and colors and kinds
(and the animals of every shape and color in the great ocean)
are each distinct? All of them without exception
(not one is not)
come about from the good and unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental karma created by the mind.”
The Sutra of the Buddha Speaks the Five Sufferings says:

“The mind takes hold of hell, the mind takes hold of hungry ghosts, the mind takes hold of animals, the mind takes hold of gods and humans, and gives them their shapes and appearances — all are the doing of the mind. One who can tame the mind and walk the Way has the greatest power of all.
I have fought with the mind
for countless kalpas, and only now have I attained Buddhahood, walking alone through the three realms,
all of it the doing of the mind
The Mahayana Sutra of the Buddha’s Original Birth and Mind Ground Contemplation says:
“The buddhas take the Dharma as their great master, and the bodhi path is realized by cultivating the mind.”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Simply use this mind, and directly accomplish Buddhahood.”
The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:
“Becoming a Buddha is not
(is no)
apart from the present thought.”
An earlier worthy said:
“When the mad mind does not rest, its resting is bodhi.”
Question: Above you explained why one should cultivate the mind. So then, how should one cultivate the mind?
Answer: The essential purport of mind cultivation in this piece is:
awakening first and cultivation after, and the equal holding of concentration and wisdom.

[The three realms burn with anguish, like a house on fire: how can you bear to linger, willingly enduring long suffering? To escape the wheel of rebirth, nothing is better than seeking Buddhahood; and if you would seek the Buddha, the Buddha is the mind. Why seek the mind far away? It is not apart from your own body. The physical body is false, having birth and death; the true mind is like space, neither cut off nor changing. Therefore it is said: The hundred bones scatter and return to fire and wind; one thing forever lives, covering heaven and earth.]

Within the three realms, beings are scorched by many sufferings, their bodies burning and their minds afflicted, as though they were inside a dwelling ablaze with raging fire — how could you be willing to endure and linger there, willingly undergoing suffering that has no end? If you wish to leave the three realms and be freed from the wheel of rebirth, the best course is nothing other than to seek to become a Buddha; and if you would seek to become a Buddha, the Buddha is your own mind. Why must the mind be sought far away? It is right within your own body. The physical body is false, having birth and death; the true mind is like space, neither cut off nor changing. Therefore it is said: the physical body rots away and returns to fire and wind (the four elements separate); one thing (the mind) forever lives (endures forever), covering heaven and earth.

[The hundred bones] Refers to the various bones of a person, or to the whole body; here it means the whole body. [One thing forever lives, covering heaven and earth] This eternally living thing is self-nature, that is, what this text calls “mind.” (For details see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha

[Why seek the mind far away? It is not apart from your own body] This states plainly that the mind is within the body. [The four elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth takes hardness as its nature, water takes moisture as its nature, fire takes warmth as its nature, and wind takes movement as its nature. All material things in the world have these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and movement, and therefore they are called “elements.” The physical body is compounded of the four elements, and at death the four elements separate.

[Alas! People today have long been deluded. They do not know that their own mind is the true Buddha, and do not know that their own nature is the true Dharma. They would seek the Dharma and so push it far off onto the sages, and would seek the Buddha and so fail to look into their own minds. If one says that there is a Buddha outside the mind or a Dharma outside the nature, and firmly clings to this sentiment while seeking the Buddha Way, then though one pass through dust-mote kalpas, burning one’s body, refining one’s arms, pounding out one’s bones and marrow, pricking blood to write sutras, sitting long and never lying down, eating but one meal at the hour of the rabbit, and even reciting the whole great canon and cultivating all manner of austerities, it is like steaming sand to make rice: it only adds to one’s own toil. Yet if you but know your own mind, the dharma gates numerous as the sands of the Ganges and immeasurable wondrous meanings are obtained without seeking.]

How lamentable! People of today have long been deluded. They do not know that their own mind of spiritual knowing is the true Buddha, and do not know that the empty and still self-nature is the true Dharma. They would seek the Dharma and so push it far off onto the sages (thinking that the Dharma is to be found only with the sages), and would seek to become a Buddha without contemplating their own minds (seeking the Buddha outside the mind). If one supposes that there is a Buddha outside the mind, and a Dharma outside one’s own nature, and firmly clings to this deluded sentiment while seeking the Buddha Way, then though one pass through dust-mote kalpas, burning one’s body, refining one’s arms, pounding out one’s bones and marrow, pricking blood to write sutras, sitting long and never lying down (commonly called “not lying down to rest”), eating only once a day, and even reciting the whole great canon and cultivating all manner of austerities, it is like steaming sand to make rice: it merely increases one’s own toil. You need only recognize your own mind, and the dharma gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, together with immeasurable wondrous meanings, are obtained without seeking.

[They do not know that their own nature is the true Dharma] The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says, “Self-nature can contain the ten thousand dharmas — this is greatness; the ten thousand dharmas are within the nature of every person.”

[Dust-mote kalpa] The abbreviation of the dust-mote kalpa. [The dust-mote kalpa] That is, the “three-thousand dust-mote kalpa”: one grinds all the things of a three-thousand great thousand world into ink, and every time one passes through a three-thousand great thousand world one lets fall a drop; when the ink is used up, all the worlds passed through are again crushed into fine dust, and each mote of dust is counted as one kalpa — this is a simile for a duration of time that is extremely long. [Not lying down to rest] Not sleeping at night, sitting cross-legged, whether reciting the Buddha’s name, practicing Chan, or watching a phrase, seated all day long without distinguishing day from night. [One meal] Eating only one meal a day, before noon. [The rabbit hour meal] Eating only one meal a day at the rabbit hour (six in the morning).
[Therefore the World-Honored One said: I universally behold all sentient beings, and they all possess
(ancient form of “all”)

the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue marks. He also said: All the various illusions and transformations of sentient beings are all born from the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment. From this we know that apart from this mind there is no Buddha to be accomplished. The Tathagatas of the past were only people who understood the mind; the worthy sages of the present are likewise people who cultivate the mind; those who study the Way in the future should rely on just such a Dharma. May all who cultivate the Way never seek outside. The mind-nature is undefiled, perfect from the beginning; simply be free of deluded conditions, and you are the thus-come Buddha.]

Therefore the World-Honored One said: I universally behold all sentient beings, and they all possess the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtue marks. He also said: all the various illusions and transformations of sentient beings all arise from one’s own true mind (the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment). From this we know that apart from this mind there is no Buddha to be accomplished. The buddhas of the past were only people who understood the mind; the worthy sages of the present are likewise people who cultivate the mind; those who study the Way in the future should rely on just such a Dharma, cultivating the mind and clarifying the mind, and so accomplish the Buddha Way of themselves. May all who cultivate the Way never seek outside. The mind-nature is undefiled, perfect from the beginning; so long as one no longer deludedly clings to the objects of dust, one is the dharma-body Buddha.

[Worthy and sage] One who cultivates good roots with wisdom that has outflows is called a worthy one; one who gives rise to wisdom without outflows and realizes and sees the proper principle is named a sage. Both the Great and the Small Vehicle say that one who has reached the path of seeing or above is a sage, and one before the path of seeing is a worthy one. [Wisdom with outflows] Also called worldly wisdom; that is, wisdom accompanied by afflictions. [Wisdom without outflows] The pure wisdom free of all afflictions. [The path of seeing] Cutting off the delusions of view in the three realms and seeing the principle of truth is named the path of seeing. [The principle of truth] Also called the supreme-meaning truth, the truth of the foremost meaning; that is, the true mark of all dharmas. [Deluded conditions] Deludedly clinging; here “cling” is a verb. [Simply be free of deluded conditions, and you are the thus-come Buddha] Simply be free of deluded clinging, and you are the dharma-body Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “The dharma Buddha (the dharma-body Buddha) is free of clinging.” The Diamond Sutra says: “Apart from all marks, one is named a buddha.” [The thus-come Buddha] The Buddha who awakens to the thus-come principle-essence; that is, the dharma-body Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “What is a transformation Buddha? What is a reward-born Buddha? What is the thus-come Buddha?”

[Question: If it is said that buddha-nature is present in this body, then since it is within the body and not apart from the ordinary being, why is it that I now do not see buddha-nature? Please explain this further, so that all may be brought to awakening.]

Question: If it is said that buddha-nature is present in this body right now, then since it is within the body, it should also be present in the body of an ordinary being — why is it that I now do not see buddha-nature? Please explain this further for us, so that everyone may awaken.
[Buddha-nature] In this piece, buddha-nature is a synonym for self-nature.

[Answer: It is within your own body; it is you yourself who do not see it. In the twelve periods of the day, you know hunger and you know thirst, you know cold and you know heat, you are sometimes angry and sometimes pleased — just what is it that does this? Moreover, the physical body is a compound of the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is dull and insentient — how could it see, hear, sense, and know? That which can see, hear, sense, and know must be your buddha-nature.]

Answer: Buddha-nature is within your body; it is you yourself who do not see it. In the twenty-four hours of the day, the one that knows hunger and knows thirst, knows cold and knows heat, is sometimes angry and sometimes pleased — just what thing is it? (This means: in the twenty-four hours of the day, that which knows hunger and thirst, knows cold and heat, and is sometimes angry and sometimes pleased is your buddha-nature.) Moreover, the physical body is compounded of the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is dull and insentient — how could it see, hear, sense, and know? That which can see, hear, sense, and know must surely be your buddha-nature.

[The twelve periods] In ancient times, a day and a night were divided into twelve periods. [Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing] The collective term for the consciousness-mind coming into contact with outer objects. That is: the function of eye-consciousness is seeing, the function of ear-consciousness is hearing, the function of the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body is sensing, and the function of mind-consciousness (the sixth consciousness) is knowing.
This passage of instruction means: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are likewise the functioning of buddha-nature (self-nature). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“Self-nature can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and is named the storehouse consciousness; if it gives rise to deliberation, it is the turning consciousness. It produces the six consciousnesses and issues from the six gates, seeing the six objects of dust; thus the eighteen realms all arise as functions of self-nature. If self-nature is perverse, it gives rise to eighteen perversities; if self-nature is upright, it gives rise to eighteen uprightnesses. If the use is evil, it is the use of an ordinary being; if the use is good, it is the use of a Buddha. From what does the use come? It comes from self-nature.”
(In the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, buddha-nature, the true mind, and self-nature are synonyms. For the concepts of self-nature and buddha-nature, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
Question:
What is the difference between spiritual knowing and the knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing?
Answer: Spiritual knowing is the knowing of the original mind
whereas the knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is the knowing of the consciousness-mind.

“Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing” is the collective term for the consciousness-mind coming into contact with outer objects. That is: the function of eye-consciousness is seeing, the function of ear-consciousness is hearing, the function of the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body is sensing, and the function of mind-consciousness (the sixth consciousness) is knowing. The original mind is the primordial state of mind: spiritually luminous, penetrating and clear, standing alone in its own right. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“One who does not know the original mind gains no benefit from studying the Dharma. If one knows the original mind and sees one’s own nature, one is named a true person, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”

The consciousness-mind is also called the clinging-mind — the mind that arises by clinging to and discriminating the six objects of dust; it is what the Buddha in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment calls the “shadows of the conditions of the six objects of dust.” Its characteristic is discrimination, calculation, liking and disliking, taking and rejecting. The arising of thoughts and the stirring of mind, and seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing (the “knowing” here is discriminative knowing) — all these are the consciousness-mind at work. The original mind is undefiled, and so it is also called the intrinsically pure mind. The original mind is without knowing and yet omniscient, and therefore the original mind is also called the mind of spiritual knowing. Note carefully: the “knowing” of spiritual knowing is a knowing without grasping at marks; in order to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and perceiving, it is called spiritual knowing. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:
“Prajna is non-knowing — that is, it is without the knowing that grasps at marks.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“To establish knowing upon seeing and hearing is the root of ignorance; when seeing and hearing are without the mark of seeing, this is nirvāṇa, undefiled and truly pure.”
Practice is to settle this scattered consciousness-mind (the clinging-mind) and thereby arrive at the state of the original mind (the mind of spiritual knowing) — as it is said,
“when the mad mind does not rest, its resting is bodhi.”
The Essential Methods of Mind Transmission says:
“When thoughts cease and deliberation is forgotten, the Buddha appears of himself.”
The Sutra of the Buddha Treasury says:
“The buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is entirely without thought and without conception.”

“Therefore Master Linji said: ‘The four great elements do not understand speaking and hearing the Dharma, and empty space does not understand speaking and hearing the Dharma; only this present, clear, solitary radiance in you, without form or segment, truly understands speaking and hearing the Dharma.’ What is called ‘without form or segment’ is the Dharma seal of all Buddhas, and is also your original mind. Since buddha-nature is now present in your own body, why seek it from outside? If you do not believe, I shall briefly cite the causes and conditions by which the ancient sages entered the Way, so as to remove your doubt; you must earnestly believe it.”

Therefore Master Linji said: ‘The four great elements do not understand speaking and hearing the Dharma, and empty space does not understand speaking and hearing the Dharma; then who does? Only the single ray of spirit-light within you, shining alone and without form, truly understands speaking and hearing the Dharma.’ This ‘without form’ is the Dharma seal of all Buddhas, and is likewise your original mind (buddha-nature). Since buddha-nature is now present in your own body, what need is there to seek Buddhahood outside? If you do not believe, I shall briefly cite below the causes and conditions by which the ancient sages entered the Way, so that you may remove doubt; you must truly believe it.

[Clearly, distinctly] Clear and unmistakable. [Without form or segment] Without physical form. [Dharma seal] The seal of the Dharma; this is the standard of the Dharma. Whatever does not accord with the Dharma seal is not the Dharma. [Entering the Way] First recognizing true suchness — seeing one’s nature — and stepping onto the proper path of practice.

“In the past, King Yijian asked the Venerable Boluoti: ‘What is Buddha?’ The venerable said: ‘Seeing the nature is Buddha.’ The king asked: ‘Has the master seen the nature?’ The venerable said: ‘I have seen buddha-nature.’ The king asked: ‘Where is the nature?’ The venerable said: ‘The nature is in its functioning.’ The king asked: ‘What functioning? I do not see it now.’ The venerable said: ‘The functioning is present now; it is the king himself who does not see it.’ The king asked: ‘Does it exist in me?’ The venerable said: ‘If the king functions, there is nothing that is not it; if the king does not function, the essence too is hard to see.’ The king asked: ‘When it functions, in how many places does it appear?’ The venerable said: ‘When it appears there are eight.’ The king said: ‘Then tell me of these eight appearances.’ The venerable said: ‘In the womb it is called the body; in the world it is called a person; in the eye it is seeing; in the ear it is hearing; in the nose it distinguishes scents; in the tongue it speaks; in the hand it grasps; in the foot it runs. Spread everywhere, it encompasses all worlds; gathered in, it is contained in a single grain of dust. Those who know recognize it as buddha-nature; those who do not call it the spirit-soul.’ Hearing this, the king’s mind opened to awakening.”

In the past, King Yijian asked the Venerable Boluoti: ‘Which one is Buddha?’ The venerable said: ‘The nature that is able to see is Buddha.’ The king asked: ‘Master, have you seen buddha-nature?’ The venerable said: ‘I have seen buddha-nature.’ The king asked: ‘Where is buddha-nature?’ The venerable said: ‘Buddha-nature is in functioning.’ The king asked: ‘What functioning? I do not see it.’ The venerable said: ‘Buddha-nature is functioning right now; it is the king himself who does not see it.’ The king asked: ‘Can I see buddha-nature?’ The venerable said: ‘If the king functions, then you can see it (this is to know the essence through its function, just as air has no form and the eye cannot see it, yet when the air moves one feels the wind and knows that air exists); if the king does not function, the essence too is hard to see.’ The king asked: ‘When it functions, at how many places does buddha-nature appear?’ The venerable said: ‘When buddha-nature appears, there are eight kinds of circumstance.’ The king said: ‘Since there are eight kinds of circumstance, please explain them to me.’ The venerable said: ‘Buddha-nature in the womb is called the body; in the world it is called a person; in the eye it is seeing; in the ear it is hearing; in the nose it distinguishes scents; in the tongue it speaks; in the hand it grasps; in the foot it runs. When it manifests everywhere, it embraces worlds as numberless as the sands of the Ganges (describing the greatness of buddha-nature when it manifests); when it contracts, it can be contained in a single grain of dust (describing the minuteness of buddha-nature when it contracts). Those who know recognize this as buddha-nature; those who do not call it the spirit-soul.’ When King Yijian heard this, his mind opened to awakening — he had found the master of the house.”

[Spread everywhere it encompasses all worlds; gathered in it is contained in a single grain of dust] This speaks of buddha-nature being able to be both vast and minute. [Worlds as numberless as the sands of the Ganges] Worlds as countless as the sands of the Ganges; the sands of the Ganges is a way of describing an immeasurably large number.

The General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan says: “That which is now able to speak and act, to be greedy, angry, compassionate and patient, to do good and evil, to experience suffering and joy — this is your buddha-nature; this itself is originally Buddha. Apart from this there is no other Buddha.”

“Again, a monk asked Master Guizong: ‘What is Buddha?’ Guizong said: ‘I will tell you now, but I fear you will not believe.’ The monk said: ‘The master’s sincere words — how would I dare not believe?’ The master said: ‘You yourself are it!’ The monk asked: ‘How does one guard and maintain it?’ The master said: ‘With one film in the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion.’ The monk had an insight on the spot.”

Another kōan. A monk asked Master Guizong: ‘What is Buddha?’ Master Guizong said: ‘I am telling you now, but I fear you will not believe.’ The monk said: ‘The master’s sincere words — how would I dare not believe?’ Master Guizong said: ‘You yourself are Buddha!’ The monk asked: ‘How does one guard and maintain it?’ Master Guizong said: ‘With one film in the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion.’ The monk was suddenly awakened on the spot.

[Guard and maintain] To protect and to let go spontaneously; these are the two stages of removing habitual tendencies after seeing one’s nature. ‘Protecting’ is doing one’s utmost to tend the embryo of sagehood so that it is not harmed; ‘letting go spontaneously’ is when, the embryo of sagehood having grown and already able to protect itself, one follows circumstances and operates naturally, further tempering oneself amid favorable and adverse conditions so as to accomplish the four kinds of patience. Take quitting drugs as an analogy: the first stage is to stay far away from all drugs — this is protecting. When the addiction has been completely overcome, one must live an ordinary life so that even if drugs are within easy reach one is not moved by them. [Four kinds of patience] The patience of subduing, the patience of gentle compliance, the patience of non-arising, and the patience of still extinction. The patience of subduing is that of a beginning practitioner who, wishing to endure favorable and adverse circumstances, must first tame his own mind. The patience of gentle compliance is that of one who, having long tamed his mind, meets circumstances and conditions and can endure them naturally without forced restraint; at this time the mind is gentle, soft and compliant. The patience of non-arising belongs to those in the stage of sagehood, who realize that all dharmas are originally unborn, that both sentient and insentient things arise through dependent origination and are without inherent nature, that their very substance is emptiness; and so among the nature that is without inherent nature the patience-mind is unmoved, directly realizing non-arising. The patience of still extinction belongs to sages of the fruition stage, who fully realize nirvāṇa and still extinction, so that both the moving and the still aspects accord with thusness. [With one film in the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion] The eye has the sickness of a film, and so it falsely sees many flowers falling in the sky. The empty flower (hua, old form of ‘flower’) is used in the scriptures to represent illusion. ‘With one film in the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion’ means that as long as one falsely clings to body and mind as self (one film in the eye), then false appearances (empty flowers) arise thickly. The Sūtra of Perfect Awakening says: ‘What is ignorance? Good man! All beings from beginningless time have all manner of inversion, like a confused person who mistakens the four directions, falsely taking the four great elements as the substance of the body and the shadow-image of the six sense-objects as the substance of the mind. It is like one whose eyes are diseased seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky truly has no flowers; it is the sick person who falsely grasps them. Because of this false grasping, not only is he deluded about the self-nature of empty space, he is also deluded about the true place where real flowers arise. Through this false existence, one revolves in birth and death — this is called ignorance.’”

Note here that this kōan is not about intellectual understanding. It must not be understood as: Master Guizong saying ‘You yourself are Buddha!’ and so the monk understood: ‘Ah, so I am Buddha, essentially no different from the Buddhas.’ ‘The monk had an insight on the spot’ means: in that flash of thunderbolt — ‘You yourself are Buddha!’ — when he was suddenly startled, his thinking was cut off, and thus he recognized the empty, still, luminous knowing self-nature within himself. This recognition, this spiritual comprehension, is a state of awakening that transcends language and thought. If one ponders and scrutinizes it in words, one only becomes a follower of intellectual understanding.

“The causes and conditions by which the ancient sages entered the Way cited above are clear, simple and effortless. Because of these kōans, wherever there is a place of faith and understanding, one walks hand in hand with the ancient sages.”

The causes and conditions by which the ancient sages entered the Way cited above are clear and simple, and can spare a great deal of fuss. If, because of these two kōans, there is a place of faith and understanding, then one walks hand in hand with the ancient sages.

“Question: You speak of seeing one’s nature. If one truly sees one’s nature, one is a sage and should manifest spiritual powers and transformations, being different from ordinary people. Why is it that among those who today cultivate the mind, not one manifests spiritual powers and transformations?”

Question: You speak of seeing one’s nature. If one truly sees one’s nature, one is a sage and should be able to manifest spiritual powers and transformations, and be different from ordinary people. Why is it that among those who today cultivate the mind, not one is able to manifest spiritual powers and transformations?

“Answer: You must not rashly utter wild words! Not distinguishing right from wrong is that of an inverted, deluded person. Those today who study the Way talk loftily of truth with their mouths, yet in their hearts shrink back from practicing it, and so fall into the fault of having no share in seeing one’s nature — all are misled by the wrong views that trouble you. Studying the Way without knowing the order of before and after, speaking of principle without distinguishing the root from the branches — this is called wrong views, not study and practice. Not only do you mislead yourself, you also mislead others. How can one fail to be careful!”

Answer: You must not rashly utter wild words! Not distinguishing right from wrong is that of an inverted, deluded person. Those today who study the Way talk loftily of truth with their mouths, yet in their hearts shrink back from practicing it and dare not take it up, and so fall into the fault of having no share in seeing one’s nature — all are misled by these wrong views that trouble you. Studying the Way without knowing the order of before and after, speaking of principle without distinguishing the root from the branches — this is called wrong views, not study and practice. Holding such wrong views, not only do you mislead yourself, you also mislead others. How can one fail to be careful with one’s words!

“Now, there are many gates to entering the Way; to speak of it briefly, they do not go beyond two gates: sudden awakening and gradual practice. Although there is also sudden awakening and sudden practice, that is the entry of those of the highest faculties. If one traces back their past, over many lifetimes they have, relying on awakening and practicing, been gradually steeping themselves, until in this life, hearing it they are immediately awakened, and in one instant complete it all. To speak truly, they too are of the capacity that awakens suddenly and then practices gradually.”

There are many gates to entering the Way; to speak of them briefly, they do not go beyond two gates: sudden awakening and gradual practice. Although there is also sudden awakening and sudden practice, that is the entry of those of the highest faculties. Tracing back their past, over many lives they have, relying on awakening and practicing, been steeping themselves gradually, until in this life, hearing it they are immediately awakened (sudden awakening), and in one instant complete their practice. To speak truly, they are also of the capacity that awakens suddenly and then practices gradually.

“And so these two gates of sudden and gradual are the tracks of a thousand sages. Thus the sages of old, without exception, first awakened and then practiced, and only through practice attained realization. The spiritual powers and transformations you speak of are, relying on awakening and practicing, gradually manifested through steeping; it is not that they appear at the moment of awakening. As the scripture says: ‘Principle is awakened to suddenly, and riding on that awakening it is all extinguished; things are not removed suddenly, but exhausted in due sequence.’ Therefore Guifeng, deeply understanding the meaning of first awakening and then practicing, said: ‘Recognize the ice-pond as entirely water, yet borrow the warmth of the sun to melt it away; awaken that the ordinary person is already Buddha, yet rely on the power of Dharma to soak and cultivate. When the ice melts, the water flows and moistens, only then does it show the work of irrigating and washing; when false thoughts are exhausted, the mind is empty and transparent, only then does it manifest the function of illuminating radiance.’ From this one knows that spiritual powers and transformations in phenomenal matters cannot be accomplished in a single day, but manifest through gradual steeping.”

Hence these two gates of sudden awakening and gradual practice are the road walked in common by a thousand sages! Therefore the sages of old, without exception, first awakened and then practiced, and only through practice attained realization. The spiritual powers and transformations you speak of are, relying on awakening and practicing, gradually manifested through steeping; it is not that they appear at the moment of awakening. As the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: ‘Principle is awakened to suddenly, and riding on that awakening it is all extinguished; things are not removed suddenly, but exhausted in due sequence.’ Therefore Master Guifeng, deeply understanding the meaning of first awakening and then practicing, said: ‘Recognize the ice-pond as entirely water, yet borrow the warmth of the sun to melt it away; awaken that the ordinary person is already Buddha, yet rely on the power of Dharma to soak and cultivate. When the ice melts, the water flows and moistens, only then does it show the work of irrigating and washing; when false thoughts are exhausted, the mind is empty and transparent, only then does it manifest the great function of illuminating radiance.’ From this one knows that spiritual powers and transformations in phenomenal matters cannot be accomplished in a single day, but appear through gradual steeping!

[The tracks of a thousand sages] Tracks are the traces left by the wheels of a cart. ‘The tracks of a thousand sages’ means the road walked in common by a thousand sages. [Principle is awakened to suddenly, and riding on that awakening it is all extinguished; things are not removed suddenly, but exhausted in due sequence] Ultimate principle can be awakened to suddenly, and so the wrong views that take illusion as real can be extinguished riding on that awakening; but in phenomenal matters one cannot at once cease to be turned by illusion, for the habitual tendencies that take illusion as real can only be exhausted gradually, in due sequence. [Recognize the ice-pond as entirely water, yet borrow the warmth of the sun to melt it away] One suddenly understands that this pond of ice is originally water (sudden awakening), but to restore it to the state of water one must borrow the heat of the sun to gradually melt it day by day (gradual practice). [Awaken that the ordinary person is already Buddha, yet rely on the power of Dharma to soak and cultivate] One awakens that the ordinary person is originally Buddha (sudden awakening), but one must still rely on the power of Dharma to soak and cultivate before truly becoming Buddha (gradual practice).

“Moreover, spiritual powers in phenomenal matters, in the eyes of one who has penetrated, are still a matter of wizardry, and are also the marginal concern at the end of sagehood; even if they appear, one should not make use of them. The deluded fools of today falsely suppose that at the instant of a single thought of awakening, innumerable wonderful functions, spiritual powers and transformations at once appear. If one understands it this way, one is said not to know the before and after, and not to distinguish the root from the branches. Not knowing the before and after, and not distinguishing root from branch, yet seeking the Buddha Way — is like trying to fit a square peg into a round hole. Is this not a great error! Not knowing the methods of expedience, one therefore entertains the idea of a precipice, generates shrinking and retreat on one’s own, and cuts off the seeds of Buddhahood — not a few are such people. Since one is oneself unenlightened, and also does not believe in those who have understanding yet show no spiritual powers, one gives rise to contempt, deceiving the worthy and slandering the sages. How pitiable!”

Furthermore, spiritual powers in phenomenal matters, in the eyes of one who has penetrated, are still a matter of wizardry, and are the least important thing on the path to sagehood; even if spiritual powers appear, one should not value or use them. The deluded fools of today falsely suppose that at the instant of a single thought of awakening, innumerable wonderful functions, spiritual powers and transformations at once appear. If one understands it this way, one is said not to know the before and after (first one must practice gradually, and only then do spiritual powers appear) and not to distinguish the root from the branches (awakening is the root, spiritual powers are the branches). Not knowing before and after, not distinguishing root from branch, yet seeking the Buddha Way — is like trying to fit a square peg into a round hole. Is this not a great error! Not knowing the methods of practice, one therefore regards awakening as unattainably high, generates shrinking and retreat on one’s own, and so cuts off the seeds of Buddhahood in oneself; such people are everywhere. One does not understand what awakening is, and does not believe in the awakening of those awakened ones who manifest no spiritual powers, and so gives rise to contempt, deceiving the worthy and slandering the sages. How pitiable!

[It is also the marginal concern at the end of sagehood] Master Yangshan Huiji said: ‘Do not seek the three clarities and six penetrations — why? Because this is the marginal concern at the end of sagehood; now one should recognize the mind and reach the root. Only get the root, and do not worry about the branches; in time they will be present of themselves (having got the root, through gradual practice, as habitual tendencies gradually grow faint, the three clarities and six penetrations will naturally come); if one has not got the root, though one studies them with emotional consciousness, one will not attain them.’ (Record of the Five Lamps Merged) The Song of Certifying the Way says: ‘Only get the root, do not worry about the branches, like pure lapis lazuli containing the precious moon. Once one can understand this wish-fulfilling pearl, benefiting self and others never runs dry.’ [Three clarities] The clarity of past lives, the clarity of the divine eye, and the clarity of the extinction of defilements. The clarity of past lives is understanding all affairs of one’s own and others’ past lives; the clarity of the divine eye is understanding all affairs of one’s own and others’ future lives; the clarity of the extinction of defilements is, with sage wisdom, cutting off all afflictions. [Six penetrations] The heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, knowledge of others’ thoughts, the recollection of past lives, the power of spiritual locomotion, and the extinction of defilements.

“Question: You say that the two gates of sudden awakening and gradual practice are the tracks of a thousand sages. Since awakening is sudden, why need one still practice gradually? If practice is gradual, why speak of sudden awakening? Please explain further the two meanings of sudden and gradual, so as to put an end to all remaining doubt.”

Question: You say that the two gates of sudden awakening and gradual practice are the road walked in common by a thousand sages. Since awakening is sudden, why need one still practice gradually? If practice is gradual, why then speak of sudden awakening? Please explain further the two meanings of sudden and gradual, so as to cut off completely all doubt.

“Answer: As for sudden awakening, while the ordinary person is deluded, he takes the four great elements as the body and deluded thought as the mind, not knowing that the self-nature is the true Dharma body, not knowing that his own luminous knowing is the true Buddha. Seeking Buddha outside the mind, he wanders about flustered. Suddenly, being directed by a good and wise teacher onto the path, in one thought he turns the light back and sees his own nature. And this nature-ground is originally without affliction; the wisdom-nature without defilement is originally complete in itself, in no way different from the Buddhas. Therefore it is called sudden awakening.”

Answer: As for sudden awakening, while the ordinary person is deluded, he takes the four great elements as the body and deluded thought as the mind, not knowing that the self-nature is the true Dharma body, not knowing that his own luminous knowing is the true Buddha. So he seeks Buddha outside the mind, rushing east and running west. Suddenly, being directed by a good and wise teacher onto the gate of entry, in one thought he turns the light back and sees his own nature. Then he realizes that in this nature-ground there is originally no affliction, that the wisdom-nature without defilement is inherently complete, in no way different from the Buddhas. Therefore it is called sudden awakening.

[Luminous knowing] Luminous knowing is knowledge without the grasping of characteristics; to distinguish it from the knowledge of seeing, hearing and perceiving that grasps characteristics, it is called luminous knowing. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says: ‘The prajñā that is without knowing is knowledge without the grasping of characteristics.’ The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: ‘To establish knowledge upon knowing is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and views are free of seeing, that is nirvāṇa, the pure and undefiled truth.’ Master Hanshan, in his Notes on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, says: ‘The mind is still yet knowing, both true and false are left behind; this is called the self-realized sage wisdom.’ Master Yongjia, in the Collected Works of Chan Master Yongjia, the Song of Recounting the Śamatha, fourth, says: ‘After forgetting conditions, there is still sameness; the nature of luminous knowing is clearly present.’ Master Sengzhao, in his Treatise on Prajñā Without Knowing, says: ‘Because the sage mind is without knowing, therefore it knows everything. The knowing that is not knowing is called all-knowing. Therefore the scripture says: “The sage mind knows nothing, and yet knows everything.” This is trustworthy!’ (Note: in the currently circulating versions of the Cultivating the Mind Manual, some use the term ‘luminous knowing’ while others use the term ‘empty knowing’. The original text of the Cultivating the Mind Manual in this book follows No. 2020 of volume forty-eight of the Taishō Revised Tripiṭaka, The Cultivating the Mind Manual of Master Bojo of the Koryŏ Kingdom.)

“As for gradual practice, having suddenly awakened that the self-nature is no different from Buddha, the habitual tendencies from beginningless time are hard to eliminate all at once, so one relies on awakening and practices, gradually steeping to success, nurturing the embryo of sagehood, until after a long time one becomes a sage. Therefore it is called gradual practice. It is like a child on the day of birth: all his faculties are complete, no different from an adult’s, yet his strength is not yet full, and a good many years must pass before he becomes an adult.”

As for gradual practice, having suddenly awakened that one’s self-nature is in no way different from Buddha, the habitual tendencies from beginningless time are hard to eliminate all at once, so one relies on awakening and practices, gradually steeping to success, nurturing the embryo of sagehood, until after a long time one becomes a sage. Therefore it is called gradual practice. It is like a child on the day of birth: all his faculties are complete, no different from an adult’s, yet his strength is not yet full, and a good many years must pass before he grows into an adult.

[The embryo of sagehood] There are fifty-two stages of a bodhisattva’s practice up to Buddhahood: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal awakening, and wondrous awakening. The three stages of worthiness — the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications — are called the ‘embryo of sagehood’, because through cultivating the right Dharma they are nurtured and grow, until they reach the first ground and see the Way, being born into the Buddha’s family; hence the embryo of sagehood. [Three stages of worthiness] Among the fifty-two stages, the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes, the ten practices and the ten dedications have only cut off the view and thought delusions; they still have the delusions of countless dusts and the delusion of ignorance, and have not entered the sage stages of the ten grounds, so they are called only the ‘three stages of worthiness’, or ‘bodhisattvas before the grounds’.
[Sudden awakening] To suddenly awaken to the fact that this empty, still and luminous knowing mind is your original face.

“Question: What expedient means are there, such that in a single thought one turns the mind about and awakens to the self-nature? Answer: It is your own mind alone; what expedient means do you seek? If you make expedient means and further seek to comprehend, it is like a person who cannot see his own eyes, supposing he has no eyes, and further seeking to see; since these are already his own eyes, how can he see them again? If he knows they are not lost, that is seeing the eyes. With no further thought of seeking them to see, how could there be a thought of not seeing? Your own luminous knowing is likewise. Since it is your own mind, what further comprehension do you seek? If you wish to comprehend, you will not be able to; only know that you have it, and without trying to comprehend, that is seeing the nature.”

Question: What expedient means are there, such that in a single thought one turns the mind about and awakens to the self-nature? Answer: The self-nature is your own mind; what expedient means do you seek? If you make expedient means and further seek comprehension, it is like a person who cannot see his own eyes, and so supposes he has no eyes and goes looking for eyes; since he already has his own eyes, why must he see them for it to count? Only know that the eyes are not lost, and that is seeing the eyes. With no thought of seeking them to see, how could there be a thought of not seeing? Your own empty, still and luminous knowing mind is likewise; knowing it is not lost, one awakens to the self-nature. Since it is your own mind, what further comprehension do you seek? If you wish to comprehend, you will not be able to; only know that it is present and do not try to comprehend — that is seeing the nature.
[Expedient means] Skilful means, methods or words used to guide and transform sentient beings. [Comprehend] To understand, to awaken to.

“Question: Those of the highest faculties comprehend at once upon hearing it; those of the middle and lower faculties are not without doubt. Please speak further of expedient means, so that the deluded may enter in.”

Question: Those of the highest faculties comprehend at once upon hearing your words; those of the middle and lower faculties are not without doubt. Please explain more skilfully, so that the deluded may enter in.

“Answer: The Way does not belong to knowing or not-knowing. Set aside the mind that waits for awakening while still deluded, and listen to my words. All dharmas are like a dream, also like an illusion, so deluded thoughts are originally still, and sense-objects are originally empty. At the place where all dharmas are empty,
that luminous knowing is not dimmed

— this empty, still and luminous knowing mind is your original face, and is also the Dharma seal handed down in close, unbroken transmission by the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of each age, and the good and wise teachers of the world.”

Answer: The Way does not belong to knowing or not-knowing (the Way cannot be understood through thinking). Set aside the mind that waits for awakening while still deluded, and listen carefully to my words. All dharmas are like a dream, also like an illusion, so deluded thoughts are originally still, and sense-objects are originally empty. At the place where all dharmas are empty, the luminous knowing is not dimmed; this empty, still and luminous knowing mind, it is your original face, and is also the Dharma seal handed down in close, unbroken transmission by the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of each age, and the good and wise teachers of the world.

[This empty, still and luminous knowing mind is your original face] When the mind is in the state of empty stillness with luminous knowing, this is the original face of your self-nature. (In the Cultivating the Mind Manual, the mind is both function and substance. The ‘mind’ in this sentence refers to the mind-substance: this empty, still and luminous knowing mind-substance is your original face.)
“The Patriarch
(Bodhidharma)

first dwelt at Shaolin Monastery for nine years, and for the sake of the Second Patriarch, taught him only this: ‘Put to rest all conditions outside, keep the mind within without panting, make the mind like a wall — then one can enter the Way.’ Huike spoke of mind-nature in many ways, but never matched the principle; the Patriarch only refuted what was wrong
(Bodhidharma merely negated his answers)
and did not speak of
the thought-free mind-substance
(nor did he plainly state that the answer is the thought-free mind-substance)
. Then Huike suddenly said: ‘I have already put to rest all conditions
(I have already stilled all kinds of grasping)
.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Have you not fallen into annihilation?’ Huike said: ‘I have not fallen into annihilation
(the luminous knowing is clear)
.’ The Patriarch said: ‘
This is the mind-substance transmitted by all the Buddhas; doubt it no more.
The Moon Reflected in a Finger
Master Yongjia said:
“After forgetting
(losing)
conditions, there is still sameness; the nature of luminous knowing
(the mind-substance)
is clearly present
(distinctly clear)
(Collected Works of Chan Master Yongjia, the Song of Recounting the Śamatha, fourth)
[Dharma seal] The seal of the Dharma; this is the standard of the Dharma. Whatever does not accord with the Dharma seal is not the Dharma.
Master Guifeng, in the General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan, says:

“All dharmas are like a dream, so all sages say alike. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and sense-objects are originally empty. The empty and still mind, its luminous knowing not dimmed,
this empty and still knowing is your true nature
. Whether deluded or awakened
(whether deluded or awakened)
, the mind is originally self-aware
(the mind originally knows itself)

; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor on objects to appear. The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion, one falsely clings to body and mind as self and gives rise to thoughts of greed, hatred and so on. If one obtains the guidance of a good companion and suddenly awakens to this empty and still knowing, knowing that it is without thought and without form, then who is the mark of self, who is the mark of person?

Realizing that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only in this. Therefore, though one diligently practices all deeds, one takes non-thought as the sole ground.

Only attain the view of non-thought, then love and aversion naturally become faint, compassion and wisdom naturally grow bright, evil karma is naturally cut off, and merit and practice naturally increase. Having realized that all marks are not marks, one naturally practices without practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are cut off; when arising and ceasing have ceased, still illumination appears before one, functioning without end — this is called Buddha.”
The General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan also says:
(The master)
asked: ‘When all conditions are cut off, is there annihilation or not?’
(The student)
answered: ‘Though all thoughts are cut off, there is no annihilation.’
(The master)
asked: ‘By what verification do you say there is no annihilation?’
(The student)
answered: ‘I know it clearly within myself, but words cannot reach it.’ The master then confirmed
(verified)
him, saying: ‘This very thing is the self-nature pure mind; doubt it no more.’ If the answer did not accord
(did not match)
, then he merely refuted
(obstructed, negated)
the various wrongs
(the various mistaken answers)
and made him observe further; in the end he never first spoke to him of the word ‘knowing’.

He waited until he himself awakened, and then verified that he had truly personally realized the substance. Then he confirmed him, to end all remaining doubt. Therefore it is said: the mind-seal transmitted in silence.
What is called ‘silence’ is only abstaining from speaking the word ‘knowing’
(only not openly saying the word ‘knowing’)
— it is not that nothing at all is said; through the six generations the transmission was all like this. By the time of Heze
(Shenhui under the Sixth Patriarch)
, other schools vied in broadcasting, and those who sought to awaken tacitly
(if one required students to awaken in silent accord)
did not meet with the right karmic opportunity. Also, reflecting on Bodhidharma’s prophecy about a thread hanging by a hair
(original note: Bodhidharma said, ‘After the sixth generation of my Dharma, the life [of the lineage] will hang by a thread.’)
, and fearing that the essential doctrine would be cut off
(fearing that the essential doctrine of Chan would be cut off)
, he therefore plainly proclaimed ‘
the single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders

’. He left it to students to awaken more deeply or more shallowly, and made every effort to ensure that the teaching and the lineage would not be cut off. This too was that, in this land, the great Dharma — as destiny brought it about — was fit for a certain class of both clergy and laity to hear widely, and so the response was thus. As for what was transmitted in silence, others did not know it, so the robe was used as a token; as for what was transmitted openly, the students could easily recognize it, doubt being cleared merely through words; and since it was already embodied in speech, it could well be verified by citing scriptures and treatises
(since it was already embodied in speech, it could well be verified by citing scriptures and treatises)

(original note: the preceding text set forth an outer objection: ‘Do those who transmit the Dharma today speak in secret words?’ This is now the answer to it. The Dharma is the Dharma of Bodhidharma, so all who hear it benefit, deeply or shallowly. But in earlier times it was secret and now it is open, so it is not called secret words; how could one call it a different Dharma and a different teaching?)

[Through the six generations the transmission was all like this] From the First Patriarch Bodhidharma to the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, the transmission was all like this. This shows that the ‘single word “knowing”’ is the secret of the ‘mind to mind’ transmission of Chan! Master Guifeng, in his Lineage Diagram of the Mind-Dharma Transmitted by the China Mind-Dharma School, says:
“This very empty, still, mindful knowing is the empty and still mind transmitted by Bodhidharma of old.”

Question: The single word ‘knowing’ has long been a matter of dispute. Master Guifeng says: ‘The single word “knowing” is the gate of all wonders.’ Master Huanglong Sixin says: ‘The single word “knowing” is the gate of all calamities.’ Which one is right?
Answer: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To establish knowledge upon knowing is the root of ignorance.”

The first ‘knowing’ in the sentence is the gate of all wonders; if one sinks into the second ‘knowing’, it is ‘a diseased eye seeing empty flowers, and moreover inviting the flowers to bear fruit’ — this is the gate of all calamities. Master Hanshan says:

“Before the Buddha appeared in the world, before the Patriarch came from the West, the ready-made family inheritance was present, and everyone was complete in it. Because they were complete in it yet did not know it, therefore the gold-faced
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
and the blue-eyed
(Bodhidharma)

could not forbear, and gave themselves the trouble of appearing in the world to point it out to others. The million assembly on Vulture Peak, and the seventeen hundred cases of the lamp of transmission
(the seventeen hundred kōans of the Records of the Transmission of the Lamp)
