, all at a single call turned back and suddenly knew what they had always had. This is the ‘single word “knowing” being the gate of all wonders’. Alas! The Buddhas and Patriarchs originally had no concrete Dharma to give people; who would have thought that people’s diseased eyes would see empty flowers, and moreover invite the flowers to bear fruit — is this the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? This is the ‘single word “knowing” being the gate of all calamities’. If we do not again scrape the eye with a golden curette
(removing the film of the eye, so that the diseased eye does not see empty flowers; a verse says: ‘The tangled film is scraped away with the golden curette’)
, how are we to inherit
(take up, shoulder)
the family inheritance?”
(Dream Roaming Collection
the preface on sending Master Wuyan Wugong to be abbot of Shaolin Monastery) Venerable Zibo says:
“The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders; to establish knowledge upon knowing is a great calamity.”
(The Collected Works of Venerable Zibo)
[Cannot forbear] Unable to keep from smiling. ‘Cannot forbear’ — holding back a smile; ‘unable to stop oneself’ — unable to control oneself.

“If one awakens to this mind, truly it is what is called: without treading the steps of a ladder, directly ascending to the ground of Buddha; in every step transcending the three realms, on returning home suddenly cutting off all doubt. Then one can be a teacher of gods and men, compassion and wisdom mutually supporting, possessing the two benefits, worthy of the offerings of gods and men, consuming ten thousand taels of gold a day. If you are like this, you are a true great man, and the one task of your life is accomplished.”

If one awakens to this empty, still and luminous knowing mind, truly it is what is called: without treading the steps of a ladder, directly ascending to the ground of Buddha; in every step transcending the three realms, and suddenly cutting off the doubt of whether one can return home (attain Buddhahood). Then one can be a teacher of gods and men, compassion and wisdom mutually supporting, possessing the two benefits of benefitting self and others, worthy of the offerings of gods and men, able each day to consume the offerings of ten thousand taels of gold. If you are like this, you are a true great man, and the one task of your life is accomplished.

[Mutually supporting] Aiding one another. [The two benefits] Benefitting oneself and benefitting others. Seeking the Buddha-fruit above is benefitting oneself; transforming sentient beings below is benefitting others. [Consuming ten thousand taels of gold a day] This describes the greatness of one’s merit and virtue. Master Weishan says: ‘The old monk, on sitting in meditation once, can consume ten thousand taels of gold (can well receive the offerings of ten thousand taels of gold).’ [Great man] One of great resolve and great achievement, not limited by male or female.

Question: From my standpoint, what is the empty, still and luminous knowing mind? Answer: That which now asks me is your empty, still and luminous knowing mind. Why do you not turn the light back and look, still seeking it outside? I now, on your behalf, directly point to your original mind, so that you may awaken at once. You must purify your mind and listen to my words.

Question: From my standpoint, what is the empty, still and luminous knowing mind? Answer: That which you now ask me is your empty, still and luminous knowing mind. Why do you not turn your gaze back to shine inward, still seeking it outside (still asking me)? I now, with regard to you, directly point to your original mind and cause you to awaken at once. You must stop every thought (purify the mind) and listen to my words.

[You must purify the mind] This is what the Sixth Patriarch said when transmitting the Dharma to Huiming: “Do not give rise to a single thought,” “Neither think good nor think evil.” The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “‘Since you have come for the Dharma, you may set aside all conditions,
do not give rise to a single thought
, and I shall speak it for you.’ Huiming was silent for a long while; Huineng said: ‘
Neither think good nor think evil
, at just such a moment, which is the original face of the Venerable Ming?’” (For details, see
the Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

“From dawn to dusk, throughout the twelve hours, whether seeing or hearing, laughing or speaking, angered or delighted, right or wrong, in all these various activities and operations, tell me: after all, who is it that is able
(in this way)

to operate and act like this? If you say it is the physical body that operates, why is it that when someone’s thought ends at death and the body has not yet rotted, the eyes can no longer see, the ears cannot hear, the nose no longer distinguishes scents, the tongue does not speak, the body does not move, the hands do not grasp, the feet do not run? From this one knows that what is able to see, hear and act must be your original mind, not your physical body. Moreover, this physical body, in which the nature of the four great elements is empty, is like an image in a mirror or the moon in water — how could it be clearly and constantly aware, distinctly and unconfusedly know, respond and then comprehend, and possess the wonderful functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges? Therefore it is said: spiritual powers and wonderful functions — carrying water and hauling firewood.”

From dawn to dusk, throughout the twenty-four hours (the twelve two-hour periods), whether seeing or hearing, laughing or speaking, angered or delighted, right or wrong, in all these various activities and operations, tell me: after all, who is it that is able to operate and act like this? If you say that the physical body is what operates, why is it that when someone’s thought ends at death and the physical body has not yet rotted, the eyes can no longer see, the ears cannot hear, the nose no longer distinguishes scents, the tongue does not speak, the body does not move, the hands do not grasp, the feet do not run? From this one may know that what is able to see, hear and act must be your original mind, not your physical body. Moreover, this physical body is formed by a combination of the four great elements, its nature empty and dull; like an image in a mirror, or the moon in water — how could it be clearly and constantly aware, distinctly and unconfusedly know, respond and then comprehend, and possess the wonderful functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges? Therefore it is said: spiritual powers and wonderful functions — carrying water and hauling firewood — all of this comes from your original mind (Master Linji said: “Just watch the puppet on the platform, whose movement is entirely drawn by the one behind the scenes.”).

“Moreover, there are many gateways into the principle; I shall point out one gate for you, so as to lead you back to the source. Do you still hear the sound of crows crying and magpies chattering? He said: I hear it. He said: Now turn back and listen to your hearing-nature. Are there still many sounds? He said: Reaching here, all sounds and all discriminations are unobtainable. He said: Wonderful! Most wonderful! This is the gate by which Avalokiteśvara entered into the principle. I shall ask you again: you say ‘reaching here, all sounds and all discriminations are entirely unobtainable’; since they are unobtainable, at that moment is it empty space? He said: Originally it is not empty; it is distinctly clear and unconfused. He said: What then is the body of the not-empty? He said: It also has no appearance; speech cannot reach it. He said: This is the life of all Buddhas and all patriarchs; doubt it no more.”

Moreover, entering into the principle (realizing one’s self-nature) has many paths; now I shall point out one for you, so that you may return to the root and the source. Do you still hear the sound of crows crying and magpies chattering? He answered: I hear it. The master said: Now turn back and listen to your hearing-nature (that which is able to hear). Are there now still many sounds? He answered: Reaching here, all sounds and all discriminations are unobtainable. The master said: Wonderful! Most wonderful! This is the gate by which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara entered into the principle (turning the hearing back to the self-nature). I shall ask you again: you say ‘reaching here, all sounds and all discriminations are unobtainable’; since they are unobtainable, at that moment is it not empty space? He answered: Originally it is not empty; it is distinctly clear and unconfused. The master said: What is the body of this not-empty? He answered: It also has no appearance; speech cannot reach it. The master said: This is the vital life (the Dharma-body wisdom-life) of all Buddhas and all patriarchs; have no more doubt whatsoever.

[Crows crying and magpies chattering] In ancient times, the cries of crows and the chatter of magpies were the sounds heard most often, just as the various mechanical noises of the modern world are today. Therefore, when doing this experiencing practice, one may replace the crows’ cries and magpies’ chatter with the noises around one. [The gate by which Avalokiteśvara entered into the principle] The Śūraṅgama Sūtra

the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara says: ‘Turning back the hearing to hear the self-nature, the nature accomplishes the supreme Way.’ [This is the vital life of all Buddhas and all patriarchs] This is the Dharma-body wisdom-life of all Buddhas and patriarchs. Ordinary people take the physical body and deluded thoughts (the shadows of the six sense-objects in the six sense-organs) as their very lives. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: ‘All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have been in all sorts of inversion, like a confused person who changes the directions of the four quarters (for instance, taking east as west, south as north, and so on), falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body (falsely taking the physical body, a temporary combination of the four great elements, as the mark of their own body), and taking the shadows of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like the eye of one who is sick, seeing blossoms in empty space and a second moon. Good men! Empty space truly has no blossoms; it is the sick man who falsely clings to them. Because of false clinging, not only is he deluded about the self-nature of this empty space, but he is also deluded about the place where the real blossoms arise. Because of this falseness there is the revolving of birth-and-death, and therefore it is called ignorance.’ [The shadows of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced by the six sense-organs conditioning on the six sense-objects; and since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantoms of conditioning upon the six sense-objects.

Master Hanshan said: ‘In the clear, still night air, gather the mind and sit upright, turn the gaze back to shine inward; at the place of still, unconfused awareness, one sees the original face of oneself.’ (The Dream Roaming Collection, “Instructing the Student Chen Zifu”).

“Since it has no appearance, does it have large or small? Since it has no large or small, does it have boundaries? Because it has no boundaries, it has no inside or outside; because it has no inside or outside, it has no near or far; because it has no near or far, it has no this or that; with no this or that, there is no coming or going; with no coming or going, there is no birth or death; with no birth or death, there is no ancient or modern; with no ancient or modern, there is no delusion or awakening; with no delusion or awakening, there is no ordinary person or sage; with no ordinary person or sage, there is no defilement or purity; with no defilement or purity, there is no right or wrong; with no right or wrong, all names and words are unobtainable. Since all such sense-organs and sense-objects, all deluded thoughts, and even all kinds of appearances and all names and words are entirely unobtainable — is this not the originally empty and still, the originally thingless?”

Since it has no appearance, does it have large or small? Since it has no large or small, does it have boundaries? Because it has no boundaries, it has no inside or outside; because it has no inside or outside, it has no near or far; because it has no near or far, it has no this or that; with no this or that, there is no coming or going; with no coming or going, there is no birth or death; with no birth or death, there is no ancient or modern; with no ancient or modern, there is no delusion or awakening; with no delusion or awakening, there is no ordinary person or sage; with no ordinary person or sage, there is no defilement or purity; with no defilement or purity, there is no right or wrong; with no right and no wrong, then all names and words are unobtainable. Since it lacks all such sense-organs and sense-objects, lacks all deluded thoughts, and even all kinds of appearances and all names and words are unobtainable — is this not the originally empty and still, the originally without things?
[Names and words] Designations and expressions.

“However, at the place where all dharmas are empty, the luminous knowing is not dimmed; unlike insentient things, the nature itself spiritually comprehends — this is the pure mind-substance of your empty, still and luminous knowing. And this pure, empty and still mind is the supreme pure and bright mind of the Buddhas of the three times, and is also the original-source awakening-nature of all sentient beings. One who awakens to this and guards it, abides in the One and is liberated without movement; one who is deluded about this and turns away from it, departs into the six realms and revolves in birth-and-death for long kalpas.”

However, at the place where all dharmas are empty, the luminous knowing is not dimmed; unlike insentient things, the self-nature itself spiritually comprehends — this is the pure mind-substance of your empty, still and luminous knowing. And this pure, empty and still mind is the supreme pure and bright mind of the Buddhas of the three times, and is also the original-source awakening-nature of all sentient beings. One who awakens to this (the empty, still and luminous knowing mind) and guards it, abides in the One and is liberated without movement; one who is deluded about this and turns away from it, departs into the six realms (the six planes) and revolves in birth-and-death for long kalpas.

[Spiritual comprehension] Intuitive knowing that does not use thinking. [One who awakens to this and guards it] Guards it: to maintain the empty, still and luminous knowing mind. The preceding text says:
‘This empty, still and luminous knowing mind is your original face.’
[Abiding in the One] ‘Abiding’ means firmly maintaining.
‘The One’:

The One means the meaning of non-duality; the Same means the meaning of non-difference. What is neither two nor different is called the One. ‘Abiding in the One’ means firmly maintaining the One. In terms of concrete practice, it is this: do not think of good or evil, do not grasp at marks, remain the same and unmoved. The Sixth Patriarch said:

‘If you wish to know the essence of the mind, simply do not think of all good and evil; then you will naturally enter the pure mind-substance, serene and ever still, with wonderful functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges
(wonderful functions inexhaustible, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges)
(For details, see
the Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Question: How does one awaken to this and guard it?
Answer: It is precisely
as the later text says:
‘Therefore, after awakening, one must for a long time
observe
, and when a deluded thought suddenly arises, do not follow it at all. Diminish it and diminish it again, until one reaches non-action
(arriving at this stage of non-action, one need no longer observe, for even when thoughts arise one does not follow them)
, and only then is it final. The wakefully-aware ones of the whole world,
after awakening, tend their ox
— that is it.’

“Therefore it is said: One who is deluded about the one mind and goes into the six realms is departing and moving; one who awakens to the Dharma-realm and returns to the one mind is coming and still. Though delusion and awakening differ, the original source is one. Therefore it is said: What is called the Dharma is the mind of sentient beings. And this empty and still mind, in the sage it is not increased, in the ordinary person it is not decreased. Therefore it is said: In the sage’s wisdom it does not shine forth; hidden in the ordinary person’s mind it is not dimmed. Since it is not increased in the sage and not lessened in the ordinary person, how are Buddhas and patriarchs different from ordinary people? And that which makes them different from ordinary people is only that they are able to guard their own thoughts. If you can believe this thoroughly, doubt at once ceases; put forth the will of a great man, arouse true views, personally taste its flavor, and arrive by yourself at the place of self-assent — this is the place of understanding for one who cultivates the mind. There are no further stages or grades; therefore it is called sudden. As it is said, in the cause of faith being in accord with the fruition-virtue of the Buddhas, without the least difference, only then is faith accomplished.”

Therefore it is said: One who is deluded about the one mind and goes into the six realms does so because of departing and moving; one who awakens to the Dharma-realm and recovers the one mind does so because of coming and stillness. Though there is the difference of delusion and awakening, their original source is one. Therefore it is said: What is called the Way and the Dharma is the mind of sentient beings. And this empty and still mind, in the sage it is not increased, in the ordinary person it is not decreased. Therefore it is said: ‘In the sage’s wisdom it does not shine forth; hidden in the ordinary person’s mind it is not dimmed.’ Since it is not increased in the sage and not lessened in the ordinary person, how are Buddhas and patriarchs different from ordinary people? And that which makes them different from ordinary people is only that they are able to guard their own thoughts (within, not following the turning of thoughts; without, not being pulled by circumstances). If you can truly believe this, doubt at once ceases; put forth the will of a great man, display true views, personally taste its flavor, and arrive by yourself at the place of self-assent — this is the place of understanding for one who cultivates the mind. There are no further stages or grades, so it is called sudden. Believing that the virtue of buddha-nature within me in the stage of causal ground is not the least bit different from the virtue of the Buddhas in the stage of fruition-ground — only this is true faith.

[Being in accord with the fruition-virtue of the Buddhas, without the least difference] All sentient beings, though they revolve in the six realms and daily dwell amid defiling toil and affliction, turning their backs on the awakening-body, nevertheless the virtue of buddha-nature is still complete in them, in no way different from the Buddhas, only hidden and not manifested. [Fruition-virtue] The virtue of the stage of fruition. [Causal ground] From the ground of the ordinary person’s first giving rise to the mind of practice until before the perfect accomplishment of Buddhahood, this whole process is called the ‘causal ground’. [Fruition-ground] The stage of having realized the fruit of Buddhahood.
[Gradual practice] To guard this empty, still and luminous knowing mind, first protecting and then letting go, until one reaches non-action. The later text says:
‘Therefore, after awakening, one must for a long time observe, and when a deluded thought suddenly arises, do not follow it at all
(not letting it continue into a thought)
. Diminish it and diminish it again, until one reaches non-action
(arriving at this stage of non-action, one need no longer observe; deluded thoughts no longer arise, and one observes without observing)
, and only then is it final — this is the tending-the-ox practice after awakening of the wakefully-aware ones of the whole world.’
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Practice says:
‘What is called cultivation? Cultivation is guarding the mind; therefore one constantly observes the mind and at all times protects it.’

Question: Since one has awakened to this principle, and there are no longer any stages, why should one still rely on later practice, gradually steeping and gradually accomplishing? Answer: The meaning of gradual practice after awakening has already been fully explained above, but since your doubt is not yet dispelled, I may as well explain it again. You must purify your mind and listen attentively, listen attentively!

Question: Since one has already suddenly awakened to this principle, and the self-nature is originally empty and still, no different from the Buddha, with no stages whatsoever to be spoken of, why must one still, after awakening, rise to practice, gradually steeping and gradually accomplishing? Answer: The meaning of gradual practice after awakening has already been concretely explained above, yet your doubt is still not dispelled, so I may as well speak again. You must purify your mind and listen attentively, listen attentively

“Ordinary people, from beginningless vast kalpas up to the present day, have revolved in the five realms, dying and being born, firmly clinging to the mark of self, with inverted and deluded thoughts, the seeds and habits of ignorance, long formed into a nature. Although in this life they suddenly awaken that the self-nature is originally empty and still, no different from the Buddha, yet these old habits are hard to cut off all at once. Therefore, when they encounter adverse and favorable circumstances, enraged or delighted, right or wrong, they vividly arise and cease, and the defiling dust of affliction is no different from before. If one does not use the effort of prajñā, how can one confront ignorance and attain the ground of great rest and great cessation? As it is said: ‘Though sudden awakening is the same as the Buddha, the habits of many lives are deep; when the wind stops, the waves still surge; though the principle appears, thoughts still invade.’”

Ordinary people, from beginningless vast (vast, extremely long) kalpas up to the present day, have revolved in the five realms, dying and being born, firmly clinging to the mark of self, with inverted and deluded thoughts, the seeds and habits of ignorance long accumulated into a nature (becoming second nature). Although in this life they suddenly awaken that the self-nature is originally empty and still, no different from the Buddha, yet these habits of firmly clinging to the mark of self and inverted, deluded thinking, developed over beginningless kalpas, cannot be cut off in one go. Therefore, when they encounter adverse and favorable circumstances, enraged or delighted, right or wrong, they vividly arise and cease, and the defiling dust of affliction is no different from before. If one does not apply effort by means of prajñā, how can one confront ignorance and reach the stage of great rest and great cessation? As the worthies of old said: ‘Though one suddenly awakens that oneself is the same as the Buddha, yet the habits of many lives are deep and heavy, like when the wind stops and the waves still surge; though the principle of emptiness and stillness appears before one, the dusty and turbid thoughts still continue to invade.’

[The five realms] The heavens, humans, hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. If one speaks of the six realms, one adds the asuras. The reason the text does not mention them is that the asura realm is included within the realms of the heavens, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and so on. [Firmly clinging to the mark of self] Firmly clinging to the physical body and deluded thoughts as self. ‘Deluded thoughts’ here refers to all thoughts, because wherever there is thinking there is delusion. [The defiling dust of affliction] The external afflictions that can defile the mind-nature. Because afflictions are not originally present in the mind-nature but arise from external conditions, they are called ‘guests’; and because they can stain the mind-nature, like dust staining all things, they are called ‘dust’. The mind of sentient beings is originally pure by self-nature, but because it is stained by the defiling dust of affliction, it is not pure.

The Record of the Five Lamps Merged records: ‘At that time a monk asked, “Does a person who has suddenly awakened still have anything to practice?” The master (Chan Master Weishan Lingyou) said: “If one has truly awakened to the root, such a person knows for himself that practice and non-practice are words on two sides. Now, though a beginner may obtain it through conditions and in a single thought suddenly awaken to the self-principle, still there are the habits of beginningless vast kalpas that cannot be suddenly purified; one must cause him (the person) to purify thoroughly the present karmic stream-consciousness — that is practice. It is not that there is some other Dharma to cause him to practice and direct himself.”’

“Moreover, Chan Master Zonggao said: ‘Often those of keen faculties, without expending much effort, settle this matter and then give rise to the thought that it is easy, and no longer practice or refine. As time passes and the months deepen, they drift along as before, and cannot escape the turning of birth-and-death. So how can one abandon later practice because of a single period’s awakening?’ Therefore, after awakening, one must for a long time observe; when a deluded thought suddenly arises, do not follow it at all. Diminish it and diminish it again, until one reaches non-action, and only then is it final — this is the tending-the-ox practice after awakening of the wakefully-aware ones of the whole world.”

Moreover, Chan Master Dahui Zonggao said: ‘Often those of keen faculties, without expending much effort, suddenly awaken, and then give rise to the thought that it is easy, and no longer practice or refine. As time passes and the months deepen, they still drift along with the world as before, and cannot escape the six realms of birth-and-death. Therefore, how can one, on the basis of one awakening, abandon later practice?’ Therefore, after awakening one must for a long time, unremittingly, observe; when a deluded thought suddenly arises, do not follow it at all (not letting it continue into a thought). Diminish it and diminish it again, until one reaches non-action (arriving at this stage of non-action, one need no longer observe, for even when thoughts arise one does not follow them), and only then is it final — this is the tending-the-ox practice after awakening of the wakefully-aware ones of the whole world.

‘After awakening, one must for a long time observe; when a deluded thought suddenly arises, do not follow it at all. Diminish it and diminish it again, until one reaches non-action, and only then is it final — this is the tending-the-ox practice after awakening of the wakefully-aware ones of the whole world.’

This is the concrete method of gradual practice. And to be able to attain ‘long observing, not following thoughts as they arise’ one must have the skill of mind-contemplation. The method of mind-contemplation is detailed in this institute’s textbook
The Essentials of White Cloud Mind (The Treasure Manual of Mind-Contemplation)
[When a deluded thought suddenly arises, do not follow it at all] Master Guifeng, in the General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan, says:

‘Realizing that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only in this.’

(Translation: Awakening to “all marks being false and illusory”, the mind is naturally free of deluded thoughts. If a deluded thought arises, it shows that one has become dazed (like a person dozing off and dreaming daydreams in the daytime). One must at once be suddenly alert and wake up. And once one has awakened, the deluded thought at once disappears. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here!)

[Tending-the-ox practice] The Notes on the Jade Forest of the Chan Garden records: In the past, Lan’an paid a visit to Chan Master Baizhang, and after paying his respects, asked, ‘This student wishes to come to recognize the Buddha — what is it that is the Buddha?’ Baizhang said: ‘This is very much like riding an ox in search of an ox (you are the Buddha, and you still speak of coming to recognize the Buddha).’ He said: ‘After recognizing, what then (after recognizing the Buddha, what then? That is, after awakening, what then)?’ Baizhang said: ‘It is like a person riding an ox home (the self-nature returns to the root and the source).’ He said: ‘I do not know how to protect and maintain it from beginning to end (not knowing how one should protect and maintain it from beginning to end).’ Baizhang said: ‘It is like the ox-herd, who holds the staff and watches it, never letting it harm the crops of the field.’

“Though there is later practice, one has already suddenly awakened that deluded thoughts are originally empty and the mind-nature is originally pure. Therefore, in cutting off evil, one cuts off without cutting off; in practicing good, one practices without practicing — this is true practice and true cutting off. Therefore it is said: ‘Though one personally practices all the myriad deeds, one takes non-thought as the sole ground.’ Master Guifeng, judging the meaning of awakening-first and practicing-after, says: ‘Suddenly awakening to this nature, originally there is no affliction; the wisdom-nature without outflows is originally complete in itself, no different from the Buddha. One who practices in accordance with this is called the supreme-vehicle Chan, and is also called the Tathāgata’s pure Chan. If one can practice thought after thought, one will naturally gradually attain the hundreds and thousands of samādhis; what is transmitted and handed down among the followers of Bodhidharma is this Chan.’ Thus the meaning of sudden awakening and gradual practice is like the two wheels of a cart — lacking one, it cannot work.”

Though there is later practice, one has already suddenly awakened that deluded thoughts are originally empty and the mind-nature is originally pure. Therefore, in evil one must cut off, cutting off without cutting off (evil must be cut off, but one does not cling to it as real, nor dwell in marks); in good one must practice, practicing without practicing (good must be practiced, but one does not cling to it as real, nor dwell in marks) — this is true cutting off and true practice. Therefore it is said: ‘Though one perfectly practices the myriad deeds, one takes non-thought as the sole ground.’ Master Guifeng, judging the meaning of awakening-first and practicing-after, says: ‘Suddenly awakening to this nature, originally there is no affliction; the wisdom-nature without outflows is originally complete, no different from the Buddha. One who practices in accordance with this is called the supreme-vehicle Chan, and is also called the Tathāgata’s pure Chan. If one can practice thought after thought, one will naturally gradually attain the hundreds and thousands of samādhis; what is passed and transmitted among the disciples of Bodhidharma (the Patriarch Damo) is this Chan.’ Thus the meaning of sudden awakening and gradual practice is like the two wheels of a cart — lacking either one, it cannot work.

“Or if one does not know that good and evil are empty in nature, and sits stiffly without moving, suppressing the body and mind, like pressing down grass with a stone, and considers this to be cultivating the mind — this is a great delusion! Therefore it is said: ‘The śrāvaka, mind by mind, cuts off the delusions; but the mind that can cut off is a thief.’ Only contemplate carefully that killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and false speech arise from the self-nature; arising is non-arising, and on the very spot they are still — what need is there to cut them off? Therefore it is said: ‘Do not fear the rising of thoughts; only fear that awakening comes too late.’ Again it is said: ‘When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone.’ Therefore on the part of the awakened person, though there is the defiling dust of affliction, it all becomes the finest cream. Only observe that delusion has no root, that the three realms are like blossoms in empty space — like wind rolling up smoke; and that the illusory six sense-objects — like hot water melting ice.”

If one has not suddenly awakened, and does not know that good and evil are illusions (empty in nature), and so sits stiffly without moving, pressing down and subduing the body and mind — this is just like pressing down grass with a stone — and one still thinks this is cultivating the mind — that is a great mistake! Therefore Chan Master Baozhi said: ‘The śrāvaka, mind by mind, cuts off the delusions (the view-delusions and thought-delusions); but the mind that can cut off is a thief.’ One need only carefully observe that killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and false speech arise from the self-nature; arising is non-arising (empty in nature), so on the very spot they are extinguished — what need is there to cut them off? Therefore it is said: ‘Do not fear the rising of thoughts; only fear that awakening comes too late.’ Again it is said: ‘When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone.’ (If a deluded thought arises, one must at once realize that this is taking illusion for reality, being turned by illusory marks. Once one has realized this, the deluded thought at once disappears —
this is the essential point of the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā

.) Therefore, on the part of the awakened person (one who has already awakened), though there is the defiling dust of affliction, it all becomes the finest cream (the defiling dust of affliction is the training partner, the whetstone). One need only observe that the view-delusions and thought-delusions are originally nonexistent, and one knows that the three realms are like blossoms in empty space, and so afflictions vanish like the wind rolling up smoke; knowing that the six sense-objects are illusory transformations, afflictions melt like boiling water melting ice.

[Empty in nature] Also called no self-nature, absence of nature. All dharmas are illusions, like the affairs of a dream; their nature is originally empty, without any real self-substance. [Pressing down grass with a stone] To press down grass with a stone — though it may be pressed still for a time, the grass will still continue to grow. [The view-delusions and thought-delusions] The view-delusions and the thought-delusions. The view-delusions are the confusions and errors of ordinary people in their views, such as the five wrong views of the view of self, the view of extremes, the false view, the view of clinging to a view, and the view of clinging to rules and precepts. The thought-delusions are the confusions and errors of ordinary people in their thoughts, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride and doubt. These two delusions are the root of sentient beings’ drifting in the three realms and vainly undergoing birth-and-death; cutting them off, one can be free of birth-and-death and escape the three realms. [The śrāvaka, mind by mind, cuts off the delusions; but the mind that can cut off is a thief] Chan Master Baozhi’s ‘Praise of the Mahāyāna’ says: ‘The śrāvaka, mind by mind, cuts off the delusions; but the mind that can cut off is a thief. Thief and thief in turn eliminating each other, when will they finish with the original words and silence?’ (The Record of Pointing at the Moon)

[Only contemplate carefully that killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and false speech arise from the self-nature] Only carefully observe that killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and false speech arise from the self-nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: ‘Self-nature can contain all dharmas, so it is called the store-consciousness. If it gives rise to reflection, then it is the transforming consciousness, producing the six consciousnesses, going out the six gates, seeing the six sense-objects; thus the eighteen realms all function from the self-nature. If the self-nature is perverse, it produces the eighteen perverse functions; if the self-nature is upright, it produces the eighteen upright functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if the function is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.’ (Translation: Self-nature can contain all dharmas, hence it is called the store-consciousness. If self-nature gives rise to reflection, then it is the transforming consciousness, producing the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness). The six consciousnesses go out the six gates (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind) and see the six sense-objects (forms, sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, dharmas). Thus the eighteen realms (the six consciousnesses, the six gates and the six sense-objects) are all the functioning of the self-nature. If the self-nature is perverse, these eighteen realms produce the eighteen perverse functions; if the self-nature is upright, these eighteen realms produce the eighteen upright functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if it is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.)
[When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone] Master Guifeng, in the General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan, says:

‘Because of beginningless delusion, one falsely clings to body and mind as self and gives rise to thoughts of greed and hatred. If one obtains the guidance of a good friend and suddenly awakens to the empty and still knowing — and knowing that it is without thought and without form, then who is the mark of self, who is the mark of person? Realizing that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only in this.’

[Realizing that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone.] Awakening to the fact that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must at once realize that this is taking illusion for reality, being turned by illusory marks. Once one has realized this, the deluded thought at once disappears. [The finest cream (tíhú)] A milk product refined through repeated processing, foremost in flavor, foremost among medicines. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: ‘The finest cream is called the foremost and supreme flavor in the world.’ Again it says: ‘Among all medicines the finest cream is foremost, well curing the hot affliction and confusion of sentient beings.’

“If one can thus practice thought after thought, never forgetting to tend to the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā, then love and aversion naturally become faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic offenses naturally are cut off, and merit and practice naturally advance. When afflictions are exhausted, birth-and-death at once ceases. If the subtle flowing stream is forever cut off, the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment stands alone, clear and manifest; one then manifests hundreds and thousands of billions of transformation-bodies in the lands of the ten directions, responding to the workings of conditions, like the moon appearing in the highest heavens, its reflection divided among ten thousand waters; its functioning is inexhaustible, it saves the sentient beings of conditions, joyful and without worry, and is called the Great Awakened World-honored One.”

If one can thus practice thought after thought (when a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone), never forgetting to tend to the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā (how to hold samādhi and prajñā in equal balance is detailed in the next chapter), then the mind of love and aversion will naturally become faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic offenses naturally are cut off, and merit and practice naturally advance. When afflictions are exhausted, birth-and-death at once ends. If the subtle flowing stream is forever cut off, the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment stands alone, clear and manifest; then one is able to manifest hundreds and thousands of billions of transformation-bodies in the lands of the ten directions, responding to the workings of conditions, like the moon appearing in the highest heavens, its reflection divided among ten thousand waters; its functioning is inexhaustible, saving the sentient beings of conditions, joyful and without worry, and is called the Great Awakened World-honored One (the Buddha).

[Aversion (wù)] To detest; to loathe. [Compassion and wisdom] Compassion and wisdom are the two virtues indispensable to Buddhas and bodhisattvas, also called the ‘two gates of compassion and wisdom’. Wisdom is the upward seeking of bodhi, belonging to self-benefit; compassion is the downward transformation of sentient beings, belonging to benefiting others. [The subtle flowing stream]
The subtle arising and ceasing and flowing of the mind-consciousness is the mark of the ālaya-consciousness. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
When the bodhisattva’s grounds are exhausted
(having completed the ten grounds)
, the expedient means being fulfilled, and in a single thought corresponding, the awakening mind first arises and the mind has no initial mark;
because of being far from the subtle thoughts, one sees the mind-nature
(thoroughly seeing the original nature)
, and the mind is then ever-abiding, called the ultimate awakening.’
Master Guifeng says:
If the subtle flowing stream
(subtle thoughts)

is entirely still and extinct, only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment stands alone, clear and manifest; then, responding to conditions, one manifests hundreds and thousands of billions of bodies to save the sentient beings of conditions, and this is called Buddha.’
(See the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era)

[Like the moon appearing in the highest heavens, its reflection divided among ten thousand waters] Just as the bright moon hangs high in the sky, its reflection pervades ten thousand waters. [The highest heavens] The highest place in the sky.

blocks.text: 5.  Equal Holding of Samādhi and Prajñā

inline.s: Non-thought is samādhi; awareness of that non-thought is prajñā.
The Cultivating the Mind Manual uses the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā to subdue afflictions and to cut off afflictions
, and even to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. The preceding text says:

‘If one can thus practice thought after thought, never forgetting to tend to the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā, then love and aversion naturally become faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic offenses naturally are cut off, and merit and practice naturally advance. When afflictions are exhausted, birth-and-death at once ceases. If the subtle flowing stream is forever cut off, the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment stands alone, clear and manifest; one then manifests hundreds and thousands of billions of transformation-bodies in the lands of the ten directions, responding to the workings of conditions, like the moon appearing in the highest heavens, its reflection divided among ten thousand waters; its functioning is inexhaustible, it saves the sentient beings of conditions, joyful and without worry, and is called the Great Awakened World-honored One.’
[Equal holding of samādhi and prajñā] Stillness (non-thought) and knowing (awareness of that non-thought). The Treatise on Severing Contemplation says:
‘The stilling-extinction of the mind-nature is samādhi; the constant understanding of stilling-extinction is prajñā.’

This is to say: when the mind-nature is in a state of stilling-extinction (non-thought), it is called samādhi; constantly knowing that at this time the mind-nature is in a state of stilling-extinction is called prajñā. (Put plainly,
non-thought is samādhi; awareness of that non-thought is prajñā.

) Therefore, samādhi is stillness, prajñā is knowing. Samādhi is the substance, prajñā is the function of the substance. The equal holding of samādhi and prajñā is stillness-while-knowing and knowing-while-still. This
empty and still luminous knowing is also often called ‘illumination’; the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā is stillness-while-illuminating and illumination-while-still.
Master Dayu says:
‘Stillness
(non-thought)
illumination
(awareness of that non-thought)
illuminating stillness — above all do not use effort
(without contriving, freely and spontaneously still-illuminating)
; to become a Buddha or become a patriarch, there is no other secret.’
In the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

‘All Tathāgatas, in their original arising in the causal ground, all rely on the perfect illumination of the pure awakening-mark; forever cutting off ignorance, only then do they accomplish the Buddha Way.’

Here, the pure awakening-mark is samādhi, the perfect illumination is prajñā; illuminating the pure awakening-mark is the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā. [Stillness-and-knowing] A single thought not arising (stillness), and being aware of this single thought not arising (knowing), like a pearl emitting light, which also illuminates the pearl’s own body.
Stillness (like the pearl’s body) is the substance; knowing (like the pearl’s light) is the function of the substance.

[The original arising in the causal ground] When the Buddha was originally in the causal ground. [Causal ground] From the ground of the ordinary person’s first giving rise to the mind of practice until before the perfect accomplishment of Buddhahood, this whole process is called the ‘causal ground’.
‘The woman Amrapālī asked Mañjuśrī: “Clearly knowing that birth is a non-arising Dharma, why is one still carried along by birth-and-death?” Mañjuśrī said: “Because the power is not yet full.”’

(Translation: The woman Amrapālī asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: ‘Clearly knowing that birth is a non-arising Dharma, why is one still carried along by birth-and-death?’ The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī replied: ‘This is because the power that extinguishes false clinging is not yet full.’ For details, see
the Detailed Explanation of the Direct Presentation of the True Mind

) The reason practitioners are carried along by birth-and-death is precisely that the power that extinguishes false clinging is not yet full. Therefore, the central task of the equal holding of samādhi and prajñā is to cultivate and strengthen the power that extinguishes false clinging, and thereby extinguish false thoughts. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra
Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgatas says:
‘There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; only because of false thinking and inverted clinging does one not realize it;
if one is free of false thinking
, then all-knowledge, natural knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge are attained and manifest.’
[Deluded attachment] Clinging to illusory appearances as real.
In the Treatise on Cultivating the Mind,

cultivation is to return to the source and transform the deluded mind into the true mind. Its path is sudden awakening followed by gradual practice. Sudden awakening is awakening to this empty, still, and luminous knowing mind; gradual practice is guarding this empty, still, and luminous knowing mind. First preserve it, then let it go, until one reaches effortless non-doing. Thus, when concentration and wisdom are held in equal measure,
that
is
to be constantly dwelling in the empty, still yet luminous knowing state present at the moment of seeing one's nature, as this chapter says:

“One who awakens to this and guards it sits in sameness and attains liberation without moving. One who is deluded about this and turns from it drifts through the six realms and revolves in samsara for long aeons.”
Answer: It is what this chapter says:
Therefore, after awakening one must for a long time watch and examine,
and when deluded thoughts suddenly arise, follow none of them at all
not letting them continue into sustained thought.
Reduce and reduce again, until reaching effortless non-doing
At this non-doing stage, no watching is needed; delusion does not arise, and one watches without watching.
; only then is it ultimate. This is the ox-herding practice after awakening carried on by the good and wise teachers of the world.”
[Deluded thoughts suddenly arising, follow none of them] Master Guifeng says in the General Preface to the Collected Commentaries on the Source of Chan:

“Realize that all marks are empty, and the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately be aware of it; being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies only in this.”

Translation: Realizing that all appearances are illusory, the mind is naturally free of deluded thoughts. If a deluded thought arises, it shows you have grown dim, as one who dozes off into a daydream. You must then rouse yourself to a clear and sudden awakening. Once you awaken, the deluded thought at once disappears. The wondrous gate of practice lies right here!
Question: What skillful means are there for entering the state of stillness that yet knows?
Answer:
Accept the present moment, be wholly present, do not turn with thoughts, and do not be drawn along by conditions.

When you are accepting the present moment, wholly present, not turning with thoughts, and not drawn along by conditions, you are in the still-yet-knowing state of seeing your nature. For more on presence, see
Awareness Chan
in the sections on the preliminary practice and on investigating Chan, the chapter on investigating the Chan of presence. Therefore,
presence is concentration, and being aware of that presence is wisdom; thus this is holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure
. This is the daily practice of one who has seen their nature, a most wonderful practice, the great perfection.

There are two gates to holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure: the gate of effortless spontaneity (concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature) and the gate of remedial practice (concentration and wisdom that follow characteristics). The former is the sudden gate; the latter is the gradual gate.

blocks.text: 1. The Sudden Gate of Concentration and Wisdom

inline.s: Below
I explain the sudden gate of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure (the gate of effortless spontaneity): effortless stillness and knowing.

[Question: In the gate of practice after awakening, the meaning of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure is not yet clear to me. Please explain it further, show it in full detail, dispel my confusion, and lead me into the gate of liberation.]

Question: In the gate of arousing practice after awakening, the meaning of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure is not yet clear to me. Please explain it further, instruct in full detail, push away the mist, and lead me into the gate of liberation.

[Answer: If we speak of the meaning of the Dharma, though there be a thousand gates for entering the principle, none of them is other than concentration and wisdom. Taking its essential outline, this is but the two meanings of substance and function within one's intrinsic nature, namely what was earlier called emptiness-stillness and luminous knowing. Concentration is the substance; wisdom is the function. Because wisdom is the function of the substance, wisdom does not depart from concentration; because concentration is the substance of the function, concentration does not depart from wisdom. When there is concentration there is wisdom, so it is still yet always knowing; when there is wisdom there is concentration, so it knows yet is always still. As Caoxi says: “When the mind-ground is not confused, that is intrinsic concentration; when the mind-ground is not deluded, that is intrinsic wisdom.” If you awaken to this,
then in effortless stillness and knowing
, with no duality between excluding and illuminating, this is the one of the sudden gate who cultivates both concentration and wisdom.]

Answer: If we speak of the meaning of the Dharma, though there be a thousand gates for entering the principle, none of them is other than holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure. Taking its essential outline, this is the two meanings of substance and function within one's intrinsic nature, namely the emptiness-stillness (substance) and luminous knowing (function) spoken of earlier. Concentration is the substance, wisdom the function. Wisdom is the function of the substance (concentration), so wisdom does not depart from concentration; concentration is the substance of the function (wisdom), so concentration does not depart from wisdom. With concentration there is wisdom, so it is still yet always knowing; with wisdom there is concentration, so it knows yet is always still. As the Sixth Patriarch Huineng of Caoxi says: “When the mind-ground is not scattered, that is intrinsic concentration; when the mind-ground is not deluded, that is intrinsic wisdom.” If you awaken to this step,
in effortless stillness and knowing
, with no duality between excluding and illuminating, then this is the cultivation of both concentration and wisdom carried on by the one of the sudden gate.
Entering the principle
To enter the principle of the true reality of all dharmas.
[The true reality of all dharmas] What is called “true reality” is the real state of things; “the true reality of all dharmas” is the real state of all dharmas. In the Buddha Treasury Sutra  ·

the second chapter on Buddha-recitation, the Buddha says: “What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without any existence.” For a detailed exposition of the true reality of all dharmas, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
article

[A thousand gates for entering the principle, none other than concentration and wisdom] Though there be a thousand gates for entering the principle, not one of them can replace holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure. That is to say, holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure is the best gate for entering the principle. [Effortless spontaneity (renyun)] To let nature take its course, without contrived effort. [Stillness and knowing (jizhi)] Still, free of thought, yet knowing, aware of that thoughtlessness. [Excluding and illuminating (zhezhao)] To break dharmas and return to emptiness is called excluding; to preserve dharmas and contemplate their meaning is called illuminating. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says: “Destruction and establishment are one; excluding and illuminating are simultaneous.” [One boundary] The absence of the distinction of self and other. The Record of the Mirror of the Source says: “Though the Dharma body and the reward body are distinguished, the true and the transformed are one boundary.”

[If one says to first use stillness upon stillness to treat the wandering of thoughts, then use alertness upon alertness to treat dullness and drowsiness, treating them in sequence and harmonizing dullness and distraction in order to enter stillness, this is the gradual gate, the practice followed by those of inferior capacity. Although it is called the equal holding of alertness and stillness, it inevitably takes stillness as its practice. How then can this be one who is done with the matter, never apart from intrinsic stillness and intrinsic knowing, cultivating both without effort? Therefore Caoxi says: “One who is self-awakened in practice does not dwell on stillness; if stillness has a before and after, this is a deluded person.”]

If one says to first use stillness upon stillness to treat wandering thoughts, then use alertness upon alertness to treat dullness and drowsiness, treating them in sequence and harmonizing dullness and distraction in order to enter stillness, this is the gradual gate, the practice followed by those of inferior capacity (those of inferior faculties). Although it is called the equal holding of alertness and stillness, it inevitably takes stillness as its practice. How could this be one who is already awakened, never apart from intrinsic stillness and intrinsic knowing, cultivating both without effort? Therefore the Sixth Patriarch Huineng of Caoxi says: “One who is self-awakened in practice does not dwell on stillness; if stillness has a before and after, this is a deluded person.”
Note: In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch says:

“Self-awakened practice does not lie in disputation; if one disputes over before and after, one is the same as a deluded person. Not cutting off the mind of victory and defeat, one increases self and dharmas, never departing from the four marks.”

Translation: Self-awakened practice does not lie in argument; if one argues over superior and inferior, one is like a deluded person. Not cutting off the mind of victory and defeat, one increases attachment to self, which shows one has not departed from the mark of self, the mark of persons, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a lifespan. The author of this text, National Master Puzhao, was a man of Goryeo, and the edition he read may have been miscopied. Yet the reading, “Self-awakened practice does not dwell on stillness; if stillness has a before and after, this is a deluded person,” also makes sense and is quite penetrating.

[Then, in the case of one who has seen through to reality, the meaning of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure does not fall into effort, is originally without doing, and has no special time or place. When seeing forms and hearing sounds, be just so; when dressing and eating, be just so; when relieving oneself, be just so; when speaking with others, be just so; and so through walking, standing, sitting, lying down, whether speaking or silent, whether joyful or angry, in all times, be one and the same. Like an empty boat riding the waves, rising and falling with them; like flowing water turning around the mountain, meeting the crooked and the straight; and moment by moment, no knowing.]

Therefore, in the case of one who has seen through to reality, the meaning of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure does not fall into effort, is originally without doing, and has no particular place or time, namely the great concentration of neither entering nor leaving spoken of in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch; see
The Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
's

“seventh chapter on past conditions.” When seeing forms and hearing sounds, be just so (still yet knowing); when dressing and eating, be just so (still yet knowing); when relieving oneself, be just so (still yet knowing); when conversing with others, be just so (still yet knowing); and so through walking, standing, sitting, lying down, whether speaking or silent, whether joyful or angry, in all times, be just so (still yet knowing). It is like
an unoccupied

boat drifting on the great sea, rising and falling with the height of the waves; and again like a stream winding around the mountain, turning with the crooked and straight of the terrain, and it does not stir the mind because of its surroundings (moment by moment, no knowing).

[Like an empty boat riding the waves, rising and falling with them, like flowing water turning around the mountain, meeting the crooked and the straight] Effortless spontaneity following conditions. [Empty boat] A boat with no one in it. From the Zhuangzi. [Moment by moment, no knowing] The “knowing” here is the second “knowing” in the passage of the Surangama Sutra, “Establishing knowing upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance.” “Moment by moment, no knowing” means: moment by moment, one does not establish knowing, that is, when a thought arises, one does not continue it.

[Today swirling in effortless spontaneity, tomorrow effortless spontaneity swirling; following along with all conditions, without obstruction or hindrance. Toward good and evil, neither cutting off nor cultivating; upright and straightforward, without falsehood; seeing and hearing in an ordinary way. Then, without opposing a single dust, why trouble with the effort of banishing and clearing away? Without a single thought giving rise to emotion, one does not borrow the power of forgetting conditions.]

Today swirling in effortless spontaneity, tomorrow effortless spontaneity swirling; following along with all conditions, without obstruction or hindrance. Toward good and evil, neither cutting off nor cultivating; plain and upright, without flattery or falsehood; seeing and hearing in an ordinary way (without giving rise to discrimination). In this way, without opposing a single dust, why trouble with the effort of banishing afflictions? Without a single thought giving rise to emotion, so one need not borrow the power of forgetting conditions.

[Swirling] Continuously churning and rolling. [Without opposing a single dust, why trouble with the effort of banishing and clearing away? Without a single thought giving rise to emotion, one does not borrow the power of forgetting conditions] The loss of self and the forgetting of emotion. Master Guifeng, in the Chart of the Transmission of the Chan Gate That Transmits the Mind of the Central Vehicle, says: “Realize that all dharmas are like a dream, originally without affair; mind and its objects are originally still, not empty only from now. Deluded into thinking they exist, one sees the flourishing and withering, the noble and base, and such things. Since these affairs exist, being at odds or in accord, love and aversion and such emotions arise. When emotion arises, one is bound by all suffering. Doing in a dream and receiving in a dream, what loss, what gain? This intelligence capable of understanding is also like a dream-mind; even if there were a dharma surpassing nirvāṇa, it too would be like a dream, like an illusion. Having already reached the reality of originally no affair, it is fitting to lose the self and forget emotion. When emotion is forgotten, the cause of suffering is cut off, and only then does one cross all suffering and calamity. This is to take the forgetting of emotion as one's practice.” [Forgetting emotion (wangqing)] The extinction of emotion. In classical texts the character wang is used for wang, meaning “to destroy.” Thus “lose the self and forget emotion” means: lose the self and extinguish emotion. “This is to take the forgetting of emotion as one's practice” means: to take extinguishing emotion, that is, extinguishing the emotions of love and aversion, as one's practice. [Forgetting conditions (wangyuan)] The extinction of conditions, that is, to silence all conditions externally.

Regarding the sudden gate of concentration and wisdom, the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin gave a teaching to Chan Master Farong (the founding patriarch of the Oxhead school) that is most splendid (see the Compendium of the Five Lamps). I quote it below:
The master (Chan Master Farong), bowing his head, asked to hear the true essentials. The patriarch (the Fourth Patriarch) said:
“The hundreds and thousands of Dharma gates all return to the square inch
(the mind)

; the wonderful virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all in the source of the mind. All the gates of precepts, gates of concentration, gates of wisdom, and spiritual powers and transformations are completely self-sufficient and never apart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic hindrances are originally empty and still; all causes and effects are like dream and illusion. There is no triple world to escape, no bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans, nature and characteristics, are all equal. The great Way is vast and empty, cutting off thought, cutting off deliberation. This suchness you have now attained, lacking nothing; how are you different from a Buddha? There is no other Dharma. Just let your mind be free and at ease; do not engage in contemplative practice, do not even clarify the mind; do not give rise to greed or anger, do not harbor worry or anxiety; be expansive and unobstructed, ranging everywhere at will. Do not do various good deeds, do not do various evil deeds. Walking, standing, sitting, lying, whatever meets the eye and whatever conditions you encounter, all are the wondrous functioning of a Buddha; joyful and without worry, therefore one is called a Buddha.”

[Source of the mind] Because the mind is the root of the ten thousand dharmas, it is called the source of the mind. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says: “If the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it; when delusion ceases, the source of the mind is empty and still, all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functioning is inexhaustible.” The Calming and Contemplation says: “Sit cross-legged with hands folded, seal the lips and tie the tongue, contemplate true reality. When the source of the mind is stilled in one, the dharma realm is equally still.” And again: “If you wish to illuminate and know, you must know the source of the mind. When the source of the mind is non-dual, then all dharmas are the same as empty space.”
The master said:
“Since you do not allow contemplative practice, when objects arise, how should the mind deal with them?”
The patriarch said:

“Conditions and objects have no good or bad; good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, from where does deluded emotion arise? Since deluded emotion does not arise, the true mind knows everywhere at will. Just let your mind be free and at ease, with no further remedy; this is called the everlasting Dharma body, without change.”

blocks.text: 2. The Gradual Gate of Concentration and Wisdom

inline.s: To maintain the state of “still yet knowing” at all times and everywhere (effortless stillness and knowing), this is the sudden gate (the gate of effortless spontaneity). If one cannot yet achieve effortless stillness and knowing, but is either distracted or drowsy, then one must first use the gradual gate (the gate of remedy) to treat distraction and drowsiness, gradually attaining the ability to maintain the state of “still yet knowing” at all times and everywhere (effortless stillness and knowing), until the practice of no-effort functioning.
[Practice of no-effort functioning] Without forcing body, speech, or mind, practicing freely and spontaneously in a natural state; this is called the practice of no-effort functioning.

Below I explain the gradual gate of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure (the gate of remedy, also called the gate that follows characteristics): the treatment of distraction and drowsiness. (See
Investigating Buddha-Recitation
in the section on holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure.)

[However, when hindrances are dense, habits heavy, contemplation feeble, and the mind floats; when the power of ignorance is great and the power of prajna small, then in the midst of good and evil realms one cannot but be exchanged between activity and stillness, and the mind is not tranquil. In such a case the effort of forgetting conditions and banishing and clearing away is indeed indispensable. As it is said: “When the six senses hold the objects and the mind does not follow conditions, that is concentration; when mind and objects are both empty and illumination is without delusion, that is wisdom.” Although this belongs to the gate that follows characteristics, the gradual gate of concentration and wisdom practiced by those of inferior capacity, yet in the gate of remedy it cannot be dispensed with.]

However, if karmic hindrances are dense, habits steep, contemplation feeble, and the mind floats while awareness stirs; if the power of ignorance is great and the power of prajna small, then in the midst of good and evil circumstances one cannot but be exchanged between the two marks of activity and stillness, and the mind cannot remain at ease. In such a case the effort of forgetting conditions and banishing and clearing away is indeed indispensable. As the ancients say: “When the six senses hold the objects and the mind does not follow clinging, that is concentration; when mind and objects are both empty and illumination is free of delusion, that is wisdom.” Although this belongs to the gate that follows characteristics (the gradual gate of concentration and wisdom), it is suitable for those of inferior faculties. This method of practice, within the gate of remedy, cannot be dispensed with. (This means one should set up teachings in accord with the capacity of beings.)

[The two marks of activity and stillness] Two aspects that things possess. Activity: events arising and proceeding. Stillness: events ending and ceasing. [Exchanged between activity and stillness] This means that the mind turns with objects.

[If agitation blazes fiercely, then first use the gate of concentration to gather the scattered in accord with principle, with the mind not following conditions, tallying with original stillness. If drowsiness is especially great, then next use the gate of wisdom to select dharmas and contemplate emptiness, illuminating without delusion, tallying with original knowing. Use concentration to treat confused thinking, and wisdom to treat the indeterminate.]

If agitation (scattered thoughts) blazes fiercely, then one should first use the gate of concentration to uphold principle and gather the scattered, making the mind not follow conditions, tallying with original stillness. If drowsiness is especially great, then one should use the gate of wisdom to select dharmas and contemplate emptiness, illuminating without delusion, tallying with original knowing. In this way, use concentration to treat confused thinking (agitation), and wisdom to treat the indeterminate (drowsiness).

[Selecting dharmas] To discriminate (distinguish) the true and false among dharmas, taking the true and discarding the false, and thereby entering bodhi. [Contemplating emptiness] To contemplate the principle that the essence of all dharmas is empty.

blocks.text: 3. Entering the Sudden through the Gradual

inline.s: Below
I explain entering the gate of effortless spontaneity (the sudden gate) through the gate of remedy (the gradual gate).

[When activity and stillness both vanish, the effort of remedy is ended. Then, facing objects, thought after thought returns to the source; meeting conditions, mind after mind tallies with the Way; cultivating both without effort, only then is one a person of no affairs. If it is so, then one may truly be called one who holds concentration and wisdom in equal measure and clearly sees the Buddha nature.]

Cultivating in this way (treating distraction and drowsiness), as days pass and the effort deepens, when the marks of activity and stillness vanish, the effort of remedy is no longer needed. Thus, facing objects, thought after thought returns to the source; meeting conditions, mind after mind tallies with the Way; cultivating both without effort, only then is one a person of no affairs. If it is so, then one may truly be called one who holds concentration and wisdom in equal measure and clearly sees the original nature!

blocks.text: 6. The Debate on Sudden and Gradual

inline.s: [Question: According to your distinction, in the gate of practice after awakening the meaning of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure has two kinds: one, concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature; two, concentration and wisdom that follow characteristics.]

Question: According to the distinction you made above, in the gate of practice after awakening the meaning of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure has two kinds: one, concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature; two, concentration and wisdom that follow characteristics.

For the gate of intrinsic nature you say: effortless stillness and knowing, originally without doing. Without opposing a single dust, why trouble with the effort of banishing afflictions? Without a single thought giving rise to emotion, one need not borrow the power of forgetting conditions. You distinguish that this is the one of the sudden gate, never apart from the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature held in equal measure.

[For the gate of intrinsic nature it says: effortless stillness and knowing, originally without doing. Without opposing a single dust, why trouble with the effort of banishing and clearing away; without a single thought giving rise to emotion, one does not borrow the power of forgetting conditions. It is distinguished and said: this is the one of the sudden gate, never apart from the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature held in equal measure.]

[For the gate that follows characteristics it says: gather the scattered in accord with principle, select dharmas and contemplate emptiness, harmonizing dullness and confusion to enter non-doing. It is distinguished and said: this is the gradual gate, the practice followed by those of inferior capacity.]

For the gate that follows characteristics you say: uphold principle and gather the scattered, select dharmas and contemplate emptiness, harmonize dullness and distraction to enter non-doing. You distinguish that this is the gradual gate, the practice followed by those of inferior faculties.
[Concerning the concentration and wisdom of these two gates, there is indeed some doubt.]
In this way, the dual cultivation of concentration and wisdom has two gates, so that students cannot but have doubts.

[If it is said to be the practice of one person, does one first rely on the gate of intrinsic nature to cultivate both concentration and wisdom, and then use the remedial effort of the gate that follows characteristics? Or does one first rely on the gate that follows characteristics to harmonize dullness and confusion, and then enter the gate of intrinsic nature? If one first relies on the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature, then there is effortless stillness and knowing, with no remedial effort at all. Why need one further take up the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics? It would be like carving patterns on a bright jade, destroying its virtue.]

If we speak of one person's practice, should one first rely on the gate of intrinsic nature to cultivate both concentration and wisdom, and then use the remedial effort of the gate that follows characteristics? Or should one first rely on the gate that follows characteristics to harmonize dullness and distraction, and then enter the gate of intrinsic nature? If one first relies on the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature, then there is effortless stillness and knowing, with no remedial effort at all. Why need one further take up the gate that follows characteristics to cultivate concentration and wisdom? This is like carving patterns on a flawless bright jade disk, which instead destroys its incomparably precious quality.
[Bright jade without flaw, carving patterns destroys its virtue] A bright jade without flaw is originally most precious, yet carving patterns on it lowers its value. “Virtue” means excellent quality.

[If one first completes the remedial effort of the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics, and then heads toward the gate of intrinsic nature, this is exactly the gradual steeping before awakening of those of inferior capacity in the gradual gate. How can it be called the one of the sudden gate, who awakens first and then practices, using the effort of no-effort?]

If one first completes the remedial effort of the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics, and then heads toward the gate of intrinsic nature, then this is exactly the pre-awakening gradual steeping of those of inferior faculties in the gradual gate. How can this be called the Chan practitioner of the sudden gate, who awakens first and then practices, using the effort of no-effort?

[If they are simultaneous, without before and after, then since the concentration and wisdom of the two gates differ in suddenness and gradualness, how can they proceed side by side at the same time? Thus the one of the sudden gate relies on the gate of intrinsic nature and, in effortless spontaneity, extinguishes effort; while the inferior capacity of the gradual gate heads for the gate that follows characteristics and toils in remedial effort.]

If one uses the gate of intrinsic nature and the gate that follows characteristics at the same time, then since the concentration and wisdom of these two gates differ in suddenness and gradualness, how can they proceed side by side? Therefore, the Chan practitioner of the sudden gate relies on the gate of intrinsic nature and, in effortless spontaneity, extinguishes effort; while the inferior capacity of the gradual gate takes up the gate that follows characteristics and toils in remedial effort.

[The capacities of the two gates, sudden and gradual, differ, and their superiority and inferiority are clear. Why then, in the gate of awakening first and practicing afterward, do you explain both kinds together? Please reconcile them for us so that doubts are cut off.]

The capacities of the two gates, sudden and gradual, differ, and their superiority and inferiority are clear. Why then, in the gate of awakening first and practicing afterward, do you teach the two kinds of concentration and wisdom at the same time? Please reconcile them for us so that doubts are cut off.

[Answer: What I have explained is clear; you yourself give rise to doubt. Generating understanding by clinging to words, you turn and give rise to more perplexity. When you grasp the meaning and forget the words, you need not trouble to press further questions.]

Answer: The explanation above is stated clearly. You yourself give rise to doubt; scrutinizing and interrogating the words, you turn and give rise to more perplexity. If you grasp the true meaning behind the words, you will not spend your effort on repeated questioning.
[Grasping the meaning, forgetting the words] Not to cling to the literal meaning of phrases so as to savor their true meaning.

[If we distinguish the practice of each of the two gates, then the one who cultivates the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature is of the sudden gate, using the effort of no-effort, operating both together in dual stillness, cultivating one's own nature, and attaining Buddhahood's own Way.
