The one who cultivates the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics is, before awakening, of the gradual gate and inferior capacity, using remedial effort, cutting off delusion moment by moment, taking stillness as practice. And the practices of these two gates, sudden and gradual, are each distinct and cannot be intermingled.]

If we speak of the practice of each of the two gates as distinguished, then the one who cultivates the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature uses the effort of no-effort of the sudden gate, operating concentration and wisdom together in dual stillness, cultivating one's own nature, and attaining Buddhahood's own Way. The one who cultivates the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics uses, before awakening, the remedial effort of the gradual gate and inferior capacity, cutting off delusion moment by moment, taking stillness as practice. And the methods of these two gates, sudden and gradual, are each distinct and cannot be intermingled or confused.

[However, that the gate of practice after awakening also discusses the remedial practice of the gate that follows characteristics is not wholly adopting the practice of the gradual capacity. It merely takes up its convenience, borrowing its road and lodging for the night.]

However, that the gate of practice after awakening also discusses the remedial practice of the gate that follows characteristics is not wholly for the sake of the gradual-gate faculties. It merely takes up its convenience, borrowing its road and lodging for the night.

[Why? In this sudden gate there are also those of superior capacity and those of inferior capacity; one cannot judge their practice by a single rule. If the afflictions are thin and the body and mind are light and at ease, departing from good in the midst of good and from evil in the midst of evil, unmoved by the eight winds, still amid the three feelings, then, relying on the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature, cultivate both without effort; in innate truth without contriving, in activity and stillness always in Chan, accomplishing the principle of naturalness. Why should one borrow the meaning of remedial practice of the gate that follows characteristics?]

Why? Because in the sudden gate there are also those of superior capacity and those of inferior capacity; one cannot lay down their path of practice in a rigid, fixed way. If the afflictions are thin and the body and mind are light and at ease, able to depart from good in the midst of good and from evil in the midst of evil, unmoved by the eight winds, still amid the three feelings, then one should rely on the concentration and wisdom of intrinsic nature, cultivate both without effort, in innate truth without contriving, in activity and stillness always in Chan, accomplishing the principle of naturalness. Why should one borrow the remedial method of the gate that follows characteristics?

[The eight winds] Gain, loss, defamation, praise, fame, ridicule, suffering, and happiness. Gain is what makes a person elated; loss is what makes a person disheartened; defamation is being slandered behind one's back; praise is being commended behind one's back; fame is being commended to one's face; ridicule is being taunted to one's face; suffering is the various pain of body and mind; happiness is the various joy of body and mind. Thus these eight are ever loved and hated by the world, and moreover they can fan the mind, so they are likened to “winds.” [The three feelings] The feeling of suffering, the feeling of happiness, and the feeling of neither suffering nor happiness.

[One who is not ill does not seek medicine. Though one has first had sudden awakening, if the afflictions are dense and the habits steadfast and heavy, so that facing objects thought after thought gives rise to emotion and meeting conditions mind after mind makes opposition, and one is killed by the dullness and confusion, obscuring the constant still-yet-knowing, then one borrows the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics, not forgetting the remedy, harmonizing dullness and confusion to enter non-doing, and this is fitting for them. Though they borrow remedial effort to temporarily adjust the habits, because they have already had sudden awakening to the originally pure mind-nature and the originally empty afflictions, they do not fall into the defiled practice of the inferior capacity of the gradual gate.]

One who is not ill does not seek medicine. (Taking medicine without illness is indeed overdoing things; yet being ill and not taking medicine is likewise not fitting.) Though one has first had sudden awakening, if the afflictions are dense and the habits steadfast and heavy, so that facing objects thought after thought gives rise to emotion and meeting conditions mind after mind makes opposition, and one is killed by the dullness and distraction, obscuring the constant still-yet-knowing, then one should borrow the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics, not forgetting the remedy, harmonizing dullness and distraction to enter non-doing, and this is most fitting for them. Though they borrow remedial effort to temporarily adjust the habits, because they have already had sudden awakening to the originally pure mind-nature and the originally empty afflictions, they do not fall into the defiled practice of the inferior capacity of the gradual gate.

[Why? If one practices before awakening, then though one works without forgetting and steeps thought after thought in practice, one gives rise to doubt at each point, unable to reach unobstructedness. Like something obstructing the breast, the mark of unease is always before one. As days pass and months deepen, when the remedial effort becomes mature, the body and mind's guest-dust comes to seem like lightness and ease; yet though there is lightness and ease, the root of doubt is not cut off, like a stone pressing down on grass, and one is still in the realm of birth and death, unable to be free. Therefore it is said: practice before awakening is not true practice.]

Why? If one practices before awakening, then though one works without forgetting and steeps thought after thought in practice, one gives rise to doubt at each point, unable to reach unobstructedness. Like something obstructing the breast, the mark of unease is always before one. As days pass and months deepen, when the remedial effort becomes mature, the body and mind's guest-dust comes to seem like lightness and ease; yet though there is lightness and ease, the root of doubt is not cut off, like a stone pressing down on grass (not fundamentally resolving the problem), and one is still in the realm of birth and death, unable to be free. Therefore it is said: practice before awakening is not true practice.

[For the awakened person, though there be the convenience of remedy, with thought after thought free of doubt, not falling into defilement, as days pass and months deepen one naturally accords with the innate wondrous nature, in effortless stillness and knowing. Thought after thought, clinging to all objects, mind after mind, forever cutting off all afflictions, never apart from intrinsic nature, holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure, accomplishing supreme bodhi. Then there is no difference from the earlier superior capacity. Thus the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics, though the practice of the gradual capacity, may for the awakened person be called turning iron into gold. If one knows it is so, then why would one have the doubt of seeing the concentration and wisdom of the two gates as having a before and after, a sequence and a second?]

For the awakened person, though one also makes use of the convenient remedial method, because thought after thought is free of doubt and one does not fall into defilement, as days pass and months deepen one naturally accords with the innate wondrous nature, in effortless stillness and knowing. Thought after thought, clinging to all objects, mind after mind, forever cutting off all afflictions, never apart from intrinsic nature, holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure, accomplishing supreme bodhi. Then there is no difference at all from the one of slightly superior capacity spoken of earlier. Thus the concentration and wisdom of the gate that follows characteristics, though the practice of the gradual-gate faculties, may for the awakened person be called turning iron into gold. If one knows it is so, then why would one have the doubt of seeing the effortless concentration and wisdom and the remedial concentration and wisdom of the two gates as having a before and after, a sequence and a second?

[Thought after thought, clinging to all objects, mind after mind, forever cutting off all afflictions] This text has already said earlier: “When deluded thoughts suddenly arise, follow none of them at all.” Therefore, though thoughts cling to objects, the mind cuts off afflictions.

[May all who cultivate the Way savor and ponder these words, and no longer harbor fox-like doubt or give rise to regression. If one is possessed of a great person's resolve and seeks supreme bodhi, apart from this what else can one rely upon? Do not cling at all to the text; directly grasp the ultimate meaning. Returning each point to yourself and tallying with the original school, the wisdom of no teacher will naturally manifest, the innate principle will be clearly present and unclouded, and the wisdom body will be accomplished, not through another's awakening.]

May all who cultivate the Way carefully savor what I have said above, and no longer doubt or give rise to regression. If one is possessed of a great person's resolve and seeks supreme bodhi, apart from this path of sudden awakening followed by gradual practice, of holding concentration and wisdom in equal measure, how can one accomplish it? Do not cling at all to phrases; instead, awaken to the true meaning they point to. Returning each point to yourself and tallying with the original nature, the wisdom of no teacher will naturally manifest, the innate principle will be clearly present and unclouded, and the wisdom body will be accomplished, not through another's awakening.

[Fox-like doubt] Doubt. It is said that foxes are full of doubt, so great doubt is called fox-like doubt. [The wisdom of no teacher] The Buddha's wisdom, self-awakened without a teacher. [Wisdom body] The body of undefiled wisdom.

[And though this wondrous purport is the inheritance of every person, unless one has from the past planted the prajna seed of wisdom and possesses the capacity of the Great Vehicle, one cannot in a single thought produce true faith. Not only do they not believe, they even slander
dú
, meaning slander)

, and such as invite in return the Interminable Hell are found everywhere. Though they do not believe and accept, once the words pass their ears and there is a temporary connection of conditions, the merit and virtue cannot be measured. As the Mind-Only Verse says: “To hear and not believe still forms the cause of the Buddha-seed; to study and not succeed still increases the blessings of humans and gods, not losing the true cause of attaining Buddhahood.” How much more so for one who hears and believes, studies and succeeds, and guards without forgetting, can their merit and virtue be measured!]

And though this wondrous purport is the inheritance of every person, unless one has from the past planted the prajna seed of wisdom and possesses the capacity of the Great Vehicle, one cannot in a single thought produce true faith. Not only do they not believe, they will even add slander, and such as invite in return the miseries of the Interminable Hell are everywhere. Though they do not believe and accept, once the words pass their ears and there is a temporary connection of conditions, the merit and virtue cannot be measured. As the great master Yongming Yanshou says in the Mind-Only Verse: “To hear and not believe still forms the cause of the Buddha-seed; to study and not succeed still increases the blessings of humans and gods, not losing the true cause of attaining Buddhahood.” How much more so for one who hears and believes, studies and succeeds, and guards it without forgetting, can their merit and virtue be measured!
[One cannot produce right faith in a single thought] The “single thought” spoken of here means having no other thought. [Jue] Its.

[Reflecting on the karma of past rebirths, one does not know how many thousands of kalpas it has been. Following the darkness, entering the Interminable Hell, undergoing all manner of suffering — again, one does not know how much. And wishing to seek the Buddha-way, one does not meet a good friend, and for long kalpas sinks into oblivion, dark and unaware, creating all manner of evil karma. Sometimes at a single thought of this, one cannot help but heave a long sigh. Can one then let it slacken and again receive former calamity? And who is it again that has caused me now to receive a human life, to be the most intelligent of all creatures, not to be blind to the path of true cultivation? Truly, this is the blind turtle meeting the log, a tiny mustard seed piercing the eye of a needle — how can such good fortune be fully told!]

Reflecting on the karma of one’s own past rebirths, one does not know how many thousands of great kalpas it has been. Sunk in darkness, entering the Interminable Hell, undergoing all manner of suffering — and again, one does not know for how long! And when one wished to seek the Buddha-way, one did not meet a good friend, so that for long kalpas one sank into oblivion, dark and unaware, creating all manner of evil karma. These scenes, recalled again and again, draw forth an unending sigh! How could one let one’s practice slacken and again receive former calamity? And who is it again that has caused me to receive a human life once more, to be the most intelligent of all creatures, not to be blind to the path of true cultivation? Truly, such an opportunity is like the blind turtle boring through the hole in the log, or a blade of tiny grass passing through the eye of a needle. Yet I have this opportunity — how fortunate, how very fortunate!

[The blind turtle meeting the log] This illustrates how extremely rare the opportunity to obtain a human body for a time truly is. The Buddha told a parable: Suppose the whole earth became a great ocean, and in it there was a blind turtle whose lifespan lasted immeasurable kalpas, and only once every hundred years did it raise its head above the surface of the sea. And on the sea there floated a single plank with a hole in it, drifting wherever the wind and waves carried it. If the blind turtle raises its head only once in a hundred years, then merely to encounter that plank is already a chance most remote, let alone to come up through the hole in the plank. And the chance for sentient beings to obtain a human body for a time is even harder than this. [A tiny mustard seed piercing a needle] To throw a blade of extremely fine grass and have it pass through the eye of a needle. This too illustrates the difficulty of obtaining a human body for a time.
Mustard: a tiny blade of grass.

[If I now give rise to cowardice, or give rise to sloth, and always keep putting it off until later — in a moment my life may be lost, and I shall fall back into the evil destinies. At the time of undergoing all manner of pain, though I wish to hear a single sentence of the Buddha-Dharma, to believe, understand, receive and uphold it, and so escape bitterness — how could I obtain it again? And when danger comes, repentance is of no avail!]

If I now give rise to cowardice, or give rise to sloth, and always think of doing it later — if in a moment my life is lost and I fall back into the evil destinies, at the time of undergoing all manner of pain, though I wish to hear a single sentence of the Buddha-Dharma, to believe, understand, receive and uphold it so as to escape bitterness, how could I obtain it? And when illness is grave and death near, regret will be of no use!

[May all who cultivate the Way not give rise to self-indulgence, nor cling to greed and lust. Be as urgent as one who puts out a fire on his own head, and never forget to tend the practice. Impermanence is swift; the body is like the morning dew, life like the setting sun. Though one lives today, tomorrow is not assured — take it to heart, take it to heart! Moreover, by conditioned good of the world alone one may still escape the painful wheel of the three evil paths and, among gods and humans, obtain a supreme reward and enjoy all manner of happiness. How much more so for this most supreme vehicle, this profoundly deep Dharma-gate: to give rise to faith even for a time, the merit thereby accomplished cannot be told in similes, not even a small part of it.]
May all who cultivate the Way
not give themselves over to self-indulgence

, nor be greedy for wealth and lustful for beauty. Be as urgent as one who puts out a fire on his own head, cultivating thought after thought, never forgetting to tend the practice. Impermanence is swift; the body is like the morning dew, life like the setting sun. Though one lives today, tomorrow is not assured — take it to heart, take it to heart! Moreover, by conditioned good of the world alone one may still escape the painful wheel of the three evil paths and, among gods and humans, obtain a supreme reward and enjoy all manner of happiness. How much more so for this most supreme vehicle, this profoundly deep Dharma-gate: to give rise to faith even for a time, the merit thereby accomplished cannot be told in similes, not even a small part of it.

[Self-indulgence] Giving oneself over to pleasure. [Greed and lust] Being greedy for wealth and lustful for beauty. [Never forget to tend] Whatever object one meets and whatever condition arises, one must tend the practice and not let it be lost. [The painful wheel] The painful fruit of birth-and-death turns on without cease; hence it is called a wheel.

[As the sutra says: “If a person were to give in charity and make offerings of the seven treasures of a three-thousand great-thousand world, so that all the sentient beings of that world were filled with them, and were further to teach and transform all the sentient beings of that world, causing them to attain the four fruits — the merit of this is immeasurable and boundless, yet it is not equal to the merit obtained by one who, for the space of a single meal, rightly contemplates this Dharma.” From this we know that this Dharma-gate of mine is the most honored and most precious, and that all other merits cannot compare with it. Therefore the sutra says: “A single moment of pure mind is the place of practice; it surpasses the building of jeweled stupas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. For the jeweled stupas in the end crumble into dust, while a single moment of pure mind accomplishes right awakening.”]

As the sutra says: “If a person were to give in charity and make offerings of the seven treasures of a three-thousand great-thousand world, so that all the sentient beings of the world where you are were filled with them, and were further to teach and transform all the sentient beings of the world where you are, causing them to attain the fruit of Arhatship — such merit, immeasurable and boundless as it is, is not equal to the merit obtained by one who, for the space of a single meal, rightly contemplates this Dharma.” From this we know that this Dharma-gate of mine is the most honored and most precious, and that all other merits cannot compare with it. Therefore the sutra says: “A single moment (a settled mind) of pure mind is the place of practice; it surpasses the building of jeweled stupas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. For the jeweled stupas in the end crumble into dust, while a single moment (a settled mind) of pure mind accomplishes right awakening.”

[May all who cultivate the Way savor and ponder these words, and take them earnestly to heart. If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life shall this body be delivered? If one does not cultivate now, for ten thousand kalpas one will go astray; if one now forces oneself to practice what is hard to practice, one will gradually find it not hard, and one’s merit and practice will advance of themselves.]

May all who cultivate the Way savor these words in fine detail and take them earnestly to heart. If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life shall this body be delivered? If one does not cultivate now, for ten thousand kalpas one will meet calamity; if one now forces oneself to practice what is hard to practice, and presses on ever deeper, then it will no longer be hard, and one’s merit and practice will naturally advance.

[Alas! People today, starving, meet with the king’s feast, and yet do not know how to begin eating; sick, they meet with the king of physicians, and yet do not know how to take the medicine. Those who do not say “What is to be done? What is to be done?” — there is nothing I can do for them! Moreover, the conditioned affairs of the world have forms that can be seen and results that can be verified, and when a person accomplishes one such thing, all exclaim how rare it is. This mind-school of mine has no form that can be observed, no shape that can be seen; the path of words is cut off, the reach of mentation is extinguished. Therefore the heavenly demons and the outside paths find no way to slander it, and the gods of the heavens and the Brahma heavens cannot praise it enough — how much less could the shallow understanding of ordinary people bear any likeness to it?]

How lamentable! People today, starving, meet with the royal feast, and yet do not know how to begin eating; sick, they meet with the king of physicians, and yet do not know how to take the medicine. Truly one does not know what to say, what to say! Moreover, the conditioned affairs of the world have forms that can be seen and results that can be verified, and when a person accomplishes one such thing he exclaims how rare it is. This mind-school of mine has no form that can be observed, no shape that can be seen; the path of words is cut off, the reach of mentation is extinguished. Therefore the heavenly demons and the outside paths find no way to slander it, and Indra with the gods of the heavens and the Brahma heavens cannot praise it enough — how much less could all the talk of ordinary people of shallow understanding bear any likeness to it?

[The mind-school] The abbreviation of the Buddha Mind-School, that is, the Chan school. [The path of words is cut off, the reach of mentation is extinguished] Ultimate truth cannot be spoken of in words, nor imagined or reasoned out by the mind.

[How pitiful! How could a frog in a well know the vastness of the great ocean, and how could a jackal roar the lion’s roar? Therefore know that in this age of the degenerate Dharma, one who hears this Dharma-gate, gives rise to the thought that it is rare, and believes, understands, receives and upholds it, has already, throughout immeasurable kalpas, served all the sages, planted all wholesome roots, and deeply formed the right cause of prajñā — such a one is of the very highest capacity. Therefore the Diamond Sutra says: “As to these very phrases, one who is able to give rise to faith should know that such a one has already planted wholesome roots before immeasurable Buddhas.” It also says: “This is spoken for those who have given rise to the Great Vehicle, spoken for those who have given rise to the most supreme vehicle.”]

How pitiful! How could a frog at the bottom of a well know the vastness of the great ocean, and how could a jackal roar the lion’s roar? Therefore know that in this age of the degenerate Dharma, one who hears this Dharma-gate, gives rise to the thought that it is rare, believes, understands, receives and upholds it, has already, throughout immeasurable kalpas, served all the sages, planted all wholesome roots, and deeply formed the right cause of prajñā — such a one is of the very highest capacity. Therefore the Diamond Sutra says: “As to these very phrases, one who is able to give rise to faith should know that such a one has already planted wholesome roots before immeasurable Buddhas.” It also says: “This sutra is spoken for those who have given rise to the Great Vehicle, spoken for those who have given rise to the most supreme vehicle.”

[Jackal] A kind of fox. It is a simile for one whose practice has not yet ripened and who yet recklessly speaks the truth. [The lion’s roar] When the Buddha speaks the Dharma he is utterly without fear, his voice shakes the ten directions, and all the demons are cowed and subdued, just as when the lion roars, the hundred beasts submit.

[May all who seek the Way not give rise to timidity, but bring forth a valiant mind. Whether one’s wholesome causes from past kalpas are there or not, one cannot know. If one does not believe that one’s lot is supreme, but is content to be low and inferior and gives rise to the thought of hardship and obstruction, and so does not cultivate now, then even if one has wholesome roots from past lives, because one cuts them off now, one will rest in that difficulty and be carried further and further away.]

May all who seek the Way not give rise to timidity, but bring forth a valiant mind. Whether one’s wholesome causes from past kalpas are there or not, one cannot know. If one does not believe that one’s own causes and conditions are supreme, but is content to be low and inferior and gives rise to thoughts of hardship and peril, and so does not cultivate now, then even if one has wholesome roots from past lives, because one cuts them off now, one comes to fear the practice as hard and stops short, and so is carried further and further away from the path of bodhi.

[Whether one’s wholesome causes from past kalpas are there or not, one cannot know] How do you know that you are not of superior capacity, one whose merit and virtue are deep and abundant? It is like a boxer born with natural talent who does not train hard himself, yet complains that he has no gift, and so always loses his bouts. [Mi] Interchangeable with “mǐ,” meaning to cease.

[Now that one has already reached the place of treasure, one must not return empty-handed; once this human body is lost, it is hard to regain in ten thousand kalpas. Be careful, I beg you! Could there be a wise person who, knowing the place of treasure, does not go to seek it, but only complains forever of being lonely and poor? If one wishes to obtain the treasure, put down this bag of skin!]

Now that one has reached the place of treasure, one must not return empty-handed; once this human body is lost, it is hard to regain even in ten thousand kalpas. Do be careful, I beg you! Could there be a wise person who, knowing the place of treasure, does not go to seek it, but only complains forever of being lonely and poor? If one wishes to obtain the treasure, put down this bag of skin (this body)!

This sentence, “If one wishes to obtain the treasure, put down this bag of skin,” is of the utmost importance. Otherwise one is like a person who holds fast to the post while trying to row the boat — nothing will ever be accomplished. Old Master Xuyun said: “This shell of ours, once the breath does not come back, is a corpse. The only reason we cannot put it down is that we prize it, and so we give rise to self and other, right and wrong, love and hate, taking and rejecting. If one firmly recognizes that this shell is a corpse, does not treasure it, and simply does not regard it as self at all, what is there that one cannot put down?” Therefore, so long as one puts down this bag of skin, the mind of itself is not defiled or attached, and no dharma is taken up — what affair could remain undone?
